en: Salutations to that Kapila, by whom— out of compassion for the world submerged in the ocean of ignorance— a boat consisting of Sāṅkhya was fashioned for the sake of crossing over. *Sāṅkhyakārikā with the Gauḍapādabhāṣya* I pay homage to that Kapila, by whom, out of compassion for the world sunk in the ocean of ignorance, a boat consisting of Sāṅkhya was provided for the purpose of crossing over.
For the benefit of my students, I shall briefly proclaim this treatise, which is concise, clear, and endowed with authoritative principles, established tenets, and logical reasons.
Because of the assault of the threefold suffering, there arises a desire to know the means for its removal.
If it is argued that [the means of knowledge] are useless with respect to what is already perceived, we say no, because [the object] is not necessarily and absolutely non-existent.
Regarding the phrase "the threefold suffering," an introduction to this Āryā verse is provided:
here, the Blessed One was the son of Brahmā named Kapila; namely—
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana; Āsuri, Kapila, Voḍhu, and likewise Pañcaśikha—
these are declared to be the seven great sages (maharṣis), the sons of Brahmā.

To Kapila were born simultaneously with him dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty. Having thus come into being, and perceiving the world sinking into blinding darkness through the succession of saṃsāra, he, moved by great compassion, spoke this knowledge of the twenty-five principles to the Brahmin Āsuri of the same lineage, who was desirous of knowing it.
From the knowledge of which the destruction of suffering occurs:
one who knows the twenty-five principles, in whatever stage of life he may dwell—whether he has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot—he is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Regarding this, they say:
"The desire to know [the means of liberation] arises from the assault of the threefold suffering.
In that context, the threefold suffering consists of the internal (ādhyātmika), the external due to other beings (ādhibhautika), and the celestial or environmental (ādhidaivika).
Therein, internal [suffering] is of two kinds: physical and mental.
Physical suffering consists of fever, dysentery, and so forth, produced by the imbalance of wind, bile, and phlegm.
Mental suffering consists of separation from the beloved, union with the unpleasant, and so forth.

The *ādhibhautika* (pertaining to other beings) is fourfold; it arises from the various classes of living beings—namely, from humans, cattle, wild animals, birds, reptiles, gadflies, mosquitoes, lice, bugs, fish, crocodiles, sharks, and stationary objects—and from those born from a womb, from eggs, from sweat, and from sprouts. The *ādhidaivika* (pertaining to divine or celestial agents) refers to that which belongs to the gods (*daiva*).
Or, that which originates from heaven (*div*) is "fate" (*daiva*); that which arises with reference to it—such as cold, heat, wind, rain, and the falling of thunderbolts—is fate.
Thus, just as inquiry (*jijñāsā*) is to be undertaken because of the recognition of the threefold suffering, where [should it be directed]?
It is directed toward the cause that destroys that [suffering].
Regarding the phrase "the cause that strikes down those three types of suffering":
if it is argued that such inquiry is useless with respect to what is seen—
if, that is, when the cause for striking down the threefold suffering is already perceived, that desire to know is useless— then [it is not so].

In that regard, for both types of internal [suffering], the internal means are indeed evident through the practice of the science of Ayurveda— such as the union with the pleasant, the avoidance of the unpleasant, and decoctions of pungent, bitter, and astringent substances— and for external [suffering], the warding off of injury through protection and so forth is evident. If you think that [the means] are useless because they are evident, it is not so.
Because [the visible cause] lacks both certainty and finality;

since there is no striking away of suffering by a visible cause that is certain (ekāntataḥ), necessary (avaśyam), and eternal (atyantataḥ), therefore one should apply the desire to know (jijñāsā)—that is, the wish to understand—toward another cause that strikes away [suffering] with certainty and finality.

If it is argued that the desire to know should be directed elsewhere because of what is seen, even from that [position] it is not so, because the scriptural (ānuśravika) cause is the striker away of the threefold suffering.

It is heard after [the direct experience], thus it is *anuśrava*; that which arises from that is *ānuśravika*, and it is established through scripture (*āgama*). As it is said: "We have drunk the Soma, we have become immortal; we have reached the light, we have found the gods.
What indeed can hostility now do to us? And what can the malice of a mortal do to the immortal?"
Once, there was a deliberation among the gods, Indra and the others:

"How might we become immortal? Having reflected thus, they said: "Since we have drunk this Soma, therefore we have become immortal"—the meaning is that we have become deathless. Furthermore, "we have attained light," meaning we have reached or obtained the light of heaven.

"We have found the divine gods; we have come to know them. And thus [he asks]: "What indeed will the enemy do to us?"—*nūnam* meaning certainly—what will the enemy, the foe, do to us? What indeed will the deception of the immortal and mortal do? For "deception" (*dhūrti*) means either old age or injury; what will it do to the immortal and mortal?

Furthermore, it is heard [in scripture] that there is an ultimate fruit through the slaughter of animals: "He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice conquers all worlds, overcomes death, overcomes evil, and overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin. Is it not the case that there is a desire to know the Veda because its stated fruits are exclusively ultimate and purposeful? It is said in reply: [The opponent objects: "But the slaughter of animals is a means to an end, and thus it is not an ultimate fruit; therefore, the desire to know the Veda is for the sake of what is purposeful. [To this we reply: No. Why? Because it is seen that even in the world, when one desires to obtain a particular object, one employs various means such as agriculture, commerce, or service, which are themselves not the ultimate fruits. Thus, since the slaughter of animals is a means to an end, it is not an ultimate fruit. Furthermore, the killing of living beings is a source of demerit (*adharma*), whereas the Aśvamedha sacrifice is a source of merit (*dharma*). Therefore, how can that which is a source of demerit be the means to a fruit that is a source of merit? Moreover, it is observed that even after performing the Aśvamedha sacrifice, some kings such as Nahuṣa fell from their celestial state. Consequently, since the Aśvamedha is seen to have a perishable fruit, it cannot be an ultimate fruit. Furthermore, the Aśvamedha is a ritual involving many subsidiary acts (*aṅga*) and is difficult to perform; thus, it is not something that everyone can perform. Therefore, because it is not accessible to all, it cannot be an ultimate fruit. For these reasons, the Aśvamedha is not an ultimate fruit. Consequently, the desire to know the Veda is not for the sake of what is purposeful. This being so, the statement that "one must desire to know Dharma" is merely a commendatory passage (*arthavāda*). [End of section 10. [The proponent replies: This is not so. Why? Because it is seen that even those who have performed the Aśvamedha sacrifice fall from heaven due to the exhaustion of their merit. However, it is heard that those who have performed the Aśvamedha do not fall. How is this so? It is said: "Those who have performed the Aśvamedha do not fall, nor do those who have drunk Soma, nor those who have offered the Gosava sacrifice. Since it is heard that they do not fall, the Aśvamedha is indeed an ultimate fruit. The revealed (ānuśravika) [path] is like that which is seen (dṛṣṭavat), for it is characterized by impurity, decay, and excess;
superior to that is the opposite, resulting from the discernment of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower. (ISk_2)
"Like the seen, so is the heard" (*dṛṣṭavadānuśravika*): it is "like the seen" (*dṛṣṭavat*) because it is equal to what is seen.
What is this "heard" (*ānuśravika*)? Why is that? Because it is joined with impurity, destruction, and excess.
It is joined with impurity due to the slaughter of animals; and thus it has been said:
Six hundred animals are sacrificed on the middle day of the horse sacrifice,
being three fewer than the number prescribed by the scriptural injunction.

Although dharma is prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, it is nevertheless joined with impurity due to its admixture [with adharma]. Just as many thousands of Indras and gods have passed away age after age through time— for time is indeed difficult to overcome.

Thus, because Indra and others are destroyed, [the world] is subject to decay; likewise, it is endowed with excellence (*atiśaya*), that is, with distinction (*viśeṣa*). Because the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) are not perceived [in others], there would be suffering for the other [who lacks them].
In this way, even the cause based on tradition (ānuśravika) is like that which is seen (dṛṣṭa).
If it is asked, "Which one, then, is superior? it is said:
"The opposite of those two is superior"; that which is the opposite of both the seen and the traditional is superior, meaning more praiseworthy.
Because it is not endowed with impurity, destruction, or superiority.

He asks, "How so? and replies: "Because of the knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower. Among these, the *vyakta* (the manifest) consists of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest: intellect (*buddhi*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the eleven organs, and the five gross elements.
The unmanifest is *pradhāna*;
the knower is the *puruṣa*.

Thus, these twenty-five principles (*tattva*) are said to consist of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower. It has been stated that from the thorough knowledge of this [comes] the highest good, as in the saying: "one who knows the twenty-five principles. // 2 //
Now, it is said: what is the distinction between the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower?
"Root Nature is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and modification;
the group of sixteen is only modification; and the Puruṣa is neither nature nor modification. (ISk 3)

The root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is the primary matter (*pradhāna*). It is called the "root-nature" because it is the root of the sevenfold group consisting of both natures and transformations; it is the root and it is a nature, hence the "root-nature," which is itself untransformed.
Because it does not arise from anything else, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is not a modification of anything.

The seven beginning with the Great One (*mahat*) are both natures and modifications. From the Great One [arises] intellect; the seven beginning with intellect are: 1) intellect, 2) ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), and 3–7) the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*). These seven are both natures and modifications.
For example:

from *pradhāna* (the primal nature) arises *buddhi* (intellect); thus, being a transformation, it is a modification (*vikāra*) of *pradhāna*. That same [intellect] produces the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense), and therefore it is a *prakṛti* (nature). The *ahaṃkāra* also arises from *buddhi*, so it is a *vikṛti* (modification); yet it produces the five *tanmātras* (subtle elements), so it is a *prakṛti*.

In that regard, the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*) arises from the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and thus it is a modification (*vikṛti*); from that, space (*ākāśa*) arises, and thus it is a primal nature (*prakṛti*). Likewise, the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*) arises from the ego, and thus it is a modification; in that way, it produces air (*vāyu*), and thus it is a primal nature.
The subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*) arises from the ego, and thus it is a modification; in that way, it produces earth (*pṛthivī*), and thus it is a primal nature.

The subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*) arises from the ego (*ahaṃkāra*); thus it is a transformation (*vikṛti*), yet as it produces fire (*tejas*), it is a primal nature (*prakṛti*). The subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*) arises from the ego; thus it is a transformation, yet as it produces water (*āpas*), it is a primal nature.
In this way, the seven beginning with the Great One (*mahat*) are both primal natures and transformations.

And the group of sixteen is the transformation (*vikāra*): the five sense organs, the five organs of action, the eleventh being the mind (*manas*), and the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*). This group of sixteen is indeed a modification; it is a transformation (*vikṛti*).
The *puruṣa*, however, is neither the primal nature (*prakṛti*) nor a transformation (*vikṛti*). (3)

Thus, among these three categories—the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower—by which and how many means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is the establishment of each accomplished, and by which specific means of valid cognition is which one established?

In this world, an object of knowledge (prameya) is established by a means of valid cognition, just as grain is measured by measures such as the *prastha*, or sandalwood and other substances by a scale.
Therefore, the means of valid cognition must be explained.
Perception, inference, and authoritative testimony—these three types of valid cognition are accepted because all means of knowledge are established through them;
for the establishment of the objects of knowledge depends upon valid cognition.

It is observed that the five sense-faculties of cognition—namely, the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—have exactly five objects corresponding to them in number: sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; specifically, the ear [perceives] sound, the skin touch, the eye form, the tongue taste, and the nose smell.
This is called "seen" (dṛṣṭa) as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Whatever object is not apprehended through direct perception (pratyakṣa) or inference (anumāna) is to be accepted on the basis of the word of a reliable person (āptavacana), such as:
"Indra is the king of the gods," "the Northern Kurus," "the apsarases in heaven," and so forth.
Furthermore, that which is not graspable by perception or inference is grasped through the word of a reliable authority (*āptavacana*). And it has been said:
"The wise know that authoritative speech is the word of a reliable person; they know a reliable person to be one whose defects have been exhausted.
One whose defects are exhausted would not speak an untrue sentence, because the cause [for such speech] is absent."
He who is devoted to his own duty, free from attachment and aversion, and is always honored by those of similar character— such a person is to be known as a trustworthy authority (āpta).
Within these means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), all means of valid cognition are established.
Jaimini [enumerates] six means of valid cognition. Now, what are those that are not means of valid cognition?

Presumption (arthāpatti), probability (sambhava), non-existence (abhāva), intuition (pratibhā), tradition (aitihya), and comparison (upamāna)—these are the six means of valid cognition. Among these, presumption is of two kinds: that which is seen and that which is heard. Of these, the seen [presumption] is as follows:
If the self-nature is apprehended in one instance, it is certainly apprehended in another as well.
As it has been heard:
"Devadatta does not eat during the day, yet he is seen to be fat; therefore, it is understood that he eats at night."
Possibility (sambhava) is as follows:
when "one prastha" is mentioned, four kuḍavas are inferred.
Non-existence (abhāva) is as follows:
Prior non-existence is characterized by the total absence of something prior to its arising; for example, Devadatta’s non-existence in childhood, youth, and so forth.
Mutual non-existence is the absence of a jar in a cloth.
Absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is like a donkey's horn, the son of a barren woman, or a flower in the sky.
Non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), which is the absence of everything, is like a burnt cloth;
just as the absence of rain is understood from seeing dry grain.
Thus, non-existence is of many kinds,
just as manifestation is:
that which is to the south of the Vindhya and to the north of the Sahya [mountains].
"That region on the earth, as far as the ocean, is delightful.
When this is said, there arises an inspired intuition (*pratibhā*) that excellent qualities exist in that region; this is what is meant by "inspired intuition" (*pratibhānvāsasaṃjñāna*).
As for tradition (*aitihya*): [it is] as follows.
The world says, "A yakṣiṇī dwells in this banyan tree"—this is tradition (aitihya).
As for analogy (upamāna): "A gavaya is like a cow; a pond is like the ocean."

These six means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are subsumed within the three categories beginning with "seen" (dṛṣṭa). Among them, presumption (arthāpatti) is subsumed under inference (anumāna); while probability (sambhava), non-existence (abhāva), intuition (pratibhā), tradition (aitihya), and analogy (upamāna) are subsumed under authoritative testimony (āptavacana).

Therefore, because all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established within these three alone, threefold means of valid cognition are accepted. He states this: "By that threefold means of valid cognition, the establishment of the means of valid cognition occurs"—this is the completion of the sentence. For the establishment of the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) results from the means of valid cognition. The objects of valid cognition are the primary principles (*tattva*): primordial matter (*pradhāna*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the eleven organs (*indriya*), the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*), and the person (*puruṣa*). These twenty-five principles are called the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower.
In that regard, some things are to be established by perception, some by inference, and some by verbal testimony; thus, the threefold means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated.
[4] What is the definition of that [perception]? To this he says:
"Perception is the determinate cognition of each respective object; inference is declared to be of three kinds."
That which is preceded by the relationship between the sign and the bearer of the sign is authoritative scripture; moreover, it is the word of a trustworthy person.
The meaning is that *dṛṣṭa* (perception) is the ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) by means of the ear and other senses regarding their respective objects, such as sound and so forth.
Inference (*anumāna*) is declared to be threefold: *śeṣavat*, *pūrvavat*, and *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*.
That which has a "prior" (*pūrva*) is *pūrvavat*; for example, one establishes rain from the rising of clouds because of its having occurred previously.
The *śeṣavat* [inference] is as follows: just as when a single *pala* of water from the ocean is found to be salty, it is inferred that the remainder also possesses the quality of salinity.
This is an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).
It is observed that [an object] has reached another location from a different location.
"The moon and stars possess motion, like Caitra.

Just as, upon seeing a person named Caitra who has arrived at another place from a different location, one concludes "he possesses motion," so too with the moon and stars; and just as, from seeing a mango tree in bloom, one infers "there are mango trees in bloom elsewhere," he establishes [the point] by means of an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).
This is the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

Furthermore, as for what is called "preceded by the mark and the bearer of the mark" (*liṅga-liṅgi-pūrvaka*), that inference is "preceded by the mark" (*liṅga-pūrvaka*) where the bearer of the mark is inferred by means of the mark, as when [one infers] a mendicant by means of his staff.

And it is "preceded by the bearer of the mark" (*liṅgi-pūrvaka*) where the mark is inferred by means of the bearer of the mark, as when, having seen a mendicant, one thinks, "this is his triple-staff."
"Reliable revelation" (āpta-śruti) and "the word of a reliable person" (āpta-vacana):
the reliable persons are the teachers, Brahmā and others;
revelation is the Veda.
The authoritative person (āpta) and the sacred scripture (śruti) constitute "authoritative revelation" (āpta-śruti); that which is spoken by them is "authoritative testimony" (āpta-vacana).

// 5 // Thus, the threefold means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has been stated. Among these, it is now explained what is to be established by which means of valid cognition: "From perception in its general form, there is the establishment of supersensuous things through inference."
Therefore, that which is unestablished and beyond the senses is established through authoritative scripture (āptāgama).

The establishment of supersensible entities—those that transcend the senses—is achieved through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) and the Spirit (*puruṣa*) are both supersensible; they are proven by inference from general observation because the mark (*liṅga*), consisting of the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest, is composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*). That of which this effect, composed of the three qualities, is the manifestation is Primordial Matter.
Because this [Pradhāna] appears as if it were conscious, there must be another, a presiding Puruṣa.

This is evident and established by direct perception. Furthermore, that which is unestablished and beyond the senses is established through authoritative scripture (āptāgama), just as the fact that Indra is the king of the gods, that there are the Northern Kurus, and that there are Apsarases in heaven—all such things beyond the senses are established by the word of an authority. // 6 //

Regarding this, someone says: "The *pradhāna* or the *puruṣa* is not perceived; and whatever is not perceived in the world does not exist, therefore these two also do not exist, just like a second head or a third arm. To this it is replied:
In this regard, even though objects exist, their perception does not occur in eight ways; namely:

due to excessive distance, due to proximity, due to injury to the sense organs, due to instability of the mind, due to subtlety, due to obstruction, due to being overwhelmed, and due to merging with similar things. (ISk 7)
In this world, it is observed that even existing objects may not be perceived due to extreme distance,
as in the case of Caitra, Maitra, and Viṣṇumitra residing in another land;
or due to extreme proximity, as when collyrium is not perceived by the eye.
Due to the impairment of the sense faculties, as in the case of the deaf and the blind, there is no perception of sound and form.
Due to the instability of the mind, as in the case of one whose mind is distracted, one does not comprehend even what is correctly spoken.
Due to subtlety, as in the case of the atoms of smoke, heat, water, and mist moving in the sky, they are not perceived.
Due to obstruction, for example, an object covered by a wall is not perceived.
Due to being overwhelmed, for example, the planets, lunar mansions, and stars are not perceived when they are eclipsed by the brilliance of the sun.

Due to being mixed with similar things, for example, a mung bean thrown into a heap of mung beans, a *kuvalaya* fruit or an *āmalaka* fruit thrown among *kuvalaya*s and *āmalaka*s, or a pigeon thrown into the midst of pigeons, is not perceived because it has been brought into contact with substances of a similar nature.

Thus, the non-perception of existing objects is seen here in eight ways. (7) And so, it may be asked: what is accepted as existing? Why is there non-perception of these two, namely *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*, and by what means is their perception achieved? It is said: their non-perception is due to subtlety (*saukṣmyāt*), not due to non-existence; their perception is through their effects (*kāryataḥ*).
And that effect, beginning with the Great One (mahat), is both dissimilar to its material cause (prakṛti) and similar to it in its essential nature.
The meaning is that the non-perception of the Pradhāna is due to its subtlety (*saukṣmyāt*).
The Pradhāna is not perceived because of its subtlety, just as smoke, heat, water, and mist particles in the sky, though they exist, are not perceived.
How, then, is it perceived?
Its apprehension is through its effect;
having seen the effect, the cause is inferred:
"The Pradhāna exists as the cause of which this is the effect."

Intellect (*buddhi*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the eleven organs (*indriya*), and the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*)—these indeed constitute its effect (*kārya*).
And that effect is dissimilar (*virūpa*) to *prakṛti*.

*Prakṛti* is the primordial matter (*pradhāna*); [the effect] is dissimilar to it, having both a nature that is unlike *prakṛti* and a nature that is similar. Likewise, in the world as well, a son is both similar to his father and dissimilar.
We shall explain later the reason why that [effect] is both similar and dissimilar.
As for this effect, such as the Great One (mahat) and so forth—is it existent in the Pradhāna or is it non-existent? This doubt arises because of the disagreement among teachers;
for in this Sāṃkhya system the effect is existent (*satkārya*), whereas for the Buddhists and others the effect is non-existent (*asatkārya*).
If it is argued that there is a contradiction in saying "if it exists, it does not come into being; if it does not exist, it does not come into being," to this he replies:

"Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because of the employment of a material cause, because of the impossibility of everything arising from everything, because the efficient cause produces only what it is capable of producing, and because of the nature of the cause, the effect pre-exists [in the cause]. (ISk 9)

Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, there is no production of both the existent and the non-existent; therefore, the effect is pre-existent (*satkārya*). In this world, there is no production of what is non-existent, just as oil cannot be produced from sand. Therefore, because the effect is produced from what is already existent, the manifest (*vyakta*) exists within the primary cause (*pradhāna*) prior to its arising; thus, the effect is pre-existent. Furthermore, because of the selection of a material cause (*upādāna*): "material cause" means the cause, and because of the selection of that [cause], in this world, whoever desires a particular thing selects that specific material cause—such as one desiring curd takes milk, but not water.
Therefore, the effect exists [in the cause].

Furthermore, because there is no production of everything from everything, nothing is produced from anything—just as gold is not produced from silver, grass, dust, or sand; therefore, because there is no production of everything from everything, the effect exists [in the cause].
And furthermore, because that which is capable produces only that which is possible.

In this world, a potter who is capable produces a jar from a lump of clay using instruments and accessories such as clay, a staff, a wheel, a cloth, a rope, and water—only because [the jar] is already potentially present; therefore, the effect exists [in the cause].
Furthermore, because of the nature of the cause, the effect exists:

whatever is the characteristic of the cause, that very same characteristic is the effect, just as barley comes from barley seeds and rice from rice seeds. If the effect were non-existent, then rice might arise from *kodrava* seeds.
And because they exist, the effect exists [in the cause].

Thus, by these five reasons, the marks such as the Great Principle (mahat) exist within the Primal Nature (pradhāna); therefore, there is the arising of the existent from the existent, not from the non-existent.
// 9 // Regarding what was stated—that the transformation is both dissimilar and similar to its material cause (prakṛti)—it is now explained how this is so.
The manifest is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, indicative, composed of parts, and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite of this.

The Manifest (vyakta), consisting of the effects beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), is "possessing a cause" (hetumat); that is, it has a cause. Upādāna, hetu, kāraṇa, and nimitta are synonyms. Pradhāna is the cause of the Manifest; therefore, the Manifest, extending down to the gross elements, is possessed of a cause. The Great Principle possesses the intellect (buddhi) as its cause; the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) possesses the Great Principle as its cause; and the five subtle elements (tanmātra) and the eleven organs possess the intellect as their cause.
It is possessed of a cause by means of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Space is possessed of a cause by means of the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*);
wind is possessed of a cause by means of the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*).
Fire has the subtle element of form as its cause;
water has the subtle element of taste as its cause;
earth has the subtle element of odor as its cause.
Thus, the manifest (vyakta), extending up to the elements (bhūta), possesses a cause.
Furthermore, it is non-eternal because it is produced from something else; for example, a jar is produced from a lump of clay, and that [jar] is non-eternal.
Moreover, it is non-pervasive—that is, not all-pervading—whereas both Pradhāna and Puruṣa are all-pervading, the manifest is not.

Furthermore, it is active; during the time of saṃsāra, it transmigrates, having resorted to the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra) which is joined with thirteen kinds of instruments (karaṇa); therefore, it is active. Furthermore, it is manifold: intellect (buddhi), ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra), the five subtle elements (tanmātra), the eleven organs, and the five gross elements, which are based upon the five subtle elements. Moreover, it is a "mark" (liṅga) because it is subject to dissolution (laya). At the time of dissolution, the five gross elements dissolve into the subtle elements; these, together with the eleven organs, dissolve into the ego-consciousness; that dissolves into the intellect (buddhi); and that dissolves into primordial matter (pradhāna). Thus it is called a "mark."
Likewise, it is possessed of parts (*sāvayava*), together with its parts—namely sound, touch, taste, form, and smell.

Furthermore, it is dependent on others (*paratantra*); it does not possess independent power over itself, just as the intellect (*buddhi*) is dependent on *pradhāna*, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is dependent on the intellect, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the sense organs are dependent on the ego-sense, and the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*) are dependent on the subtle elements.
Thus, the dependent nature (*paratantra*) has been clearly explained as being dependent on others.
Now, we shall explain the unmanifest (*avyakta*);
the unmanifest is the opposite [of the manifest].
The unmanifest (avyakta) is the opposite of these very qualities as they have been described; the manifest (vyakta), however, is said to have a cause.
For there is nothing beyond the Pradhāna from which it could arise; therefore, the unmanifest is without a cause.
Likewise, the manifest is non-eternal, whereas the unmanifest is eternal because it is unproduced—for the elements do not arise from anything other than the Pradhāna.
Furthermore, the manifest (vyakta) would be non-pervasive, whereas the unmanifest (pradhāna) is pervasive; thus the manifest would be an effect.

Likewise, the manifest is characterized by signs (liṅga), while the unmanifest is signless (aliṅga) because of its eternity. The Great One (mahat) and the other evolutes are "signs" because they dissolve into one another at the time of dissolution (pralaya), but the Pradhāna does not do so; therefore, the Pradhāna is signless. Similarly, the manifest possesses parts (sāvayava), whereas the unmanifest is partless (niravayava); for sound, touch, taste, form, and smell do not exist in the Pradhāna.
Thus, the dependent (paratantra) is manifest (vyakta), while the independent (svatantra) unmanifest (avyakta) brings itself forth.

In this way, the difference between the manifest and the unmanifest has been stated; now their similarity is being described, as it was said: "They are of the same nature. They are both composed of the three qualities (triguṇa), non-discriminative (aviveki), objective (viṣaya), common (sāmānya), insentient (acetana), and characterized by productivity (prasavadharmi).
The manifest is thus, as is the primal nature; and the person is the reverse of that.

The Manifest is composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), meaning that of which *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the three qualities. It is non-discriminative (*aviveki*), meaning that there is no discrimination within it; it does not allow for the discrimination that "this is the Manifest" and "these are the qualities," just as one cannot say "this is a cow" and "this is a horse" while they are indistinguishable. Rather, those which are the qualities are the Manifest, and that which is the Manifest are those qualities.
Likewise, the manifest is an object (*viṣaya*), meaning it is that which is to be enjoyed; this is because it serves as the object for all puruṣas.
Likewise, the manifest is common (*sāmānya*), like a slave-girl who belongs to all, because it is shared by everyone.
The manifest is insentient (*acetana*), meaning it does not perceive pleasure, pain, or delusion.

Likewise, the manifest possesses the nature of productivity; for example, from the intellect (buddhi), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is produced, and from that, the five subtle elements (tanmātra) and the eleven organs are produced; and from the subtle elements, the five gross elements arise. Thus, these properties of the manifest have been described as ending with the property of productivity. In this way, the unmanifest is similar in form to the manifest: as the manifest is, so too is the Pradhāna. In that regard, the manifest consists of the three qualities (triguṇa), and the unmanifest likewise consists of the three qualities, since this effect beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) is composed of the three qualities.
In this world, whatever is the nature of the cause, such is the nature of the effect; for example, a cloth made from black threads is itself black.

Likewise, the manifest (vyakta) is non-discriminative (aviveki), and the Pradhāna is also not distinct from the Guṇas; it is impossible to say that the Guṇas are one thing and the Pradhāna another—it is thus the Pradhāna that is non-discriminative.
Similarly, the manifest and the Pradhāna are objects (viṣaya), because they have become objects for all Puruṣas.

Likewise, the manifest is common, and the Pradhāna is also common because it is shared by all. Likewise, the manifest is insentient, and the Pradhāna is also insentient because it does not perceive pleasure, pain, and delusion. How is this inferred? For here, from an insentient lump of clay, an insentient jar is produced.
In this way, the Pradhāna is also explained.
Now, the statement "the person (puruṣa) is likewise the opposite of that" is explained.
Being the opposite of "that" means the person is the opposite of both the manifest (vyakta) and the unmanifest (avyakta).
For example, while the manifest and the unmanifest possess the three qualities (triguṇa), the Puruṣa is devoid of qualities (aguṇa).
The manifest and the unmanifest are non-discriminative, while the Puruṣa is discriminative;
likewise, the manifest and the unmanifest are objects, while the Puruṣa is not an object;
likewise, the manifest and the unmanifest are common, while the Puruṣa is not common.
The manifest and the unmanifest are insentient, whereas the Puruṣa is sentient; he perceives—that is, he is conscious of—pleasure, pain, and delusion, and therefore the Puruṣa is called "sentient.
The manifest and the Pradhāna possess the quality of productivity, whereas the Puruṣa does not possess the quality of productivity, for nothing whatsoever is produced from the Puruṣa.
Therefore it is said: "The Puruṣa is the opposite of that."

Thus it has been said: "And likewise the Puruṣa. Just as the Pradhāna was explained in the preceding Āryā verse as being causeless (*ahetumat*), so too is the Puruṣa. For instance, while the Manifest (*vyakta*) is characterized by having a cause (*hetumat*), being non-eternal (*anitya*), and so forth, the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the opposite of that; therein, the Manifest has a cause whereas the Pradhāna is causeless. And likewise the Puruṣa is causeless, because he is unproduced (*anutpādya*).
The manifest is impermanent, while the primary cause (pradhāna) is eternal; likewise, the person (puruṣa) is eternal.
He is inactive because he is all-pervading.
The manifest is manifold, while the unmanifest is one; likewise, the person is also one.
The manifest is dependent, while the unmanifest is independent; likewise, the person (puruṣa) is independent.
The manifest has a mark (liṅga), whereas the primary matter (pradhāna) is without a mark; likewise, the person is also without a mark, for he does not dissolve anywhere.

The manifest is possessed of parts, whereas the unmanifest is partless; likewise, the person (puruṣa) is also partless, for there are no constituent parts such as sound and so forth within the person. Furthermore, the manifest is dependent, while the unmanifest is independent; likewise, the person is also independent.
The meaning is that it acts according to its own power.
Thus, this similarity between the unmanifest (avyakta) and the person (puruṣa) has been explained in the preceding Āryā verse.

The similarity between the manifest (vyakta) and the primary cause (pradhāna), as well as the dissimilarity of the person, have been explained in the Prakṛti-Āryā beginning with "consisting of the three guṇas, non-discriminative," and so forth. // 11 //
In this regard, concerning that which was stated—that both the manifest and the unmanifest consist of the three *guṇas*—the following is said in order to demonstrate the nature of those *guṇas*:
"The *guṇas* consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion; their purposes are illumination, activity, and restraint; and they function through mutual suppression, support, production, and union. (ISk 12)
The qualities (*guṇa*) consist of those whose nature is pleasure, those whose nature is displeasure, and those whose nature is despondency; this means *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Among these, *sattva* is that whose nature is pleasure; "pleasure" means happiness, and its nature is that.
*Rajas* is that whose nature is displeasure.
Tamas has dejection as its essence;
dejection is delusion (moha).
Likewise, [the qualities] have illumination, activity, and restraint as their purposes.
The word *artha* signifies capacity; thus, the meaning is that *sattva* is capable of illumination.
*Rajas* is for the purpose of activity, and *tamas* is for the purpose of restraint, meaning it is capable of stability; thus, the *guṇas* have the natures of illumination, action, and stability.
Likewise, they function through mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship.
They are described as such because they mutually overcome one another, mutually support one another, mutually generate one another, are mutually paired, and function mutually.
Regarding "mutually overcoming one another": they manifest through qualities such as pleasure and displeasure by overcoming each other;
for instance, when *sattva* is predominant, then *rajas* and *tamas* are overcome by the quality of displeasure and activity, and when *tamas* [is predominant], then...
Sattva and rajas consist of dejection and stability,
respectively. Likewise, the qualities (guṇas) are mutually dependent like a binary atomic compound (dvyaṇuka),
and they give rise to one another, just as a lump of clay produces a jar.
Likewise, they are mutual pairs; just as a woman and a man are a mutual pair, so too are the *guṇas*. And it has been said:
"Sattva is the mate of rajas, and rajas is the mate of sattva;
tamas is said to be the mate of both sattva and rajas."
The meaning is that they are mutual assistants;
and they function reciprocally, because of the statement that "the qualities (guṇas) function within the qualities.

For example, a woman who is beautiful and of good character is the cause of all happiness for some, yet she is the cause of suffering for her co-wives, and she is the cause of passion for those who are lustful.

It indeed produces delusion in a being as the cause for the manifestation of *rajas* and *tamas*. Just as a king who is ever-vigilant in protecting his subjects and restraining the wicked brings about happiness for the virtuous and suffering and delusion for the wicked, so too does *rajas* produce the activity of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Likewise, *tamas*, by its own nature which consists of concealment, produces the activity of *sattva* and *rajas*, just as clouds cover the sky.

They produce happiness for the world; by means of rain, they incite the labor of cultivation in farmers, and likewise cause delusion in those separated from their lovers—thus do the qualities function through one another.
Furthermore:
Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas is stimulating and mobile; tamas is heavy and enveloping. Their functioning for a purpose is like that of a lamp.
Sattva is light and illuminating; when sattva is predominant, then the limbs become light and there is the illumination of the intellect as well as clarity of the senses.

Rajas is stimulating and mobile; it is called "stimulating" (upaṣṭambhaka) because it urges one on, manifesting like a bull that exhibits intense stimulation upon seeing another bull—such is the function of rajas.
Likewise, rajas is observed to be mobile; one whose mental state is under the influence of rajas becomes restless in mind.
When darkness is predominant, it alone veils the guru (the heavy) parts; at that time, the sense organs become covered and incapable of performing their own functions.

Here [the opponent] asks: "If the *guṇas* are mutually contradictory, how do they accomplish a single purpose by their own nature? If so, how is there an operation for the sake of an object, like a lamp—that is, how is an operation for the sake of an object desired as being similar to a lamp?"

Just as a lamp produces the illumination of objects through the conjunction of oil, flame, and wick—though these are mutually contradictory—in the same way, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, though mutually contradictory, accomplish their purpose. An internal question arises: "The Primal Nature (*pradhāna*) and the Manifest (*vyakta*) have been explained as consisting of the three *guṇas*, non-discriminative, objective, and so forth. In that regard, the Primal Nature and the perceived [evolutes] such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest consist of the three *guṇas* and are non-discriminative, etc.
And how is this understood? To that he says:
"The [qualities] such as non-discrimination are established because of the presence of the three gunas, and because of the absence of their opposite;
since the effect consists of the qualities of its cause, the Unmanifest is also established. (ISk 14)

This quality of non-discrimination and so forth is established as belonging to the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest because they consist of the three guṇas; this is proven by the Unmanifest (avyakta). Here it is said: because of the absence of its opposite, its opposite is that [Unmanifest]; the absence of that is "the absence of its opposite. Therefore, the Unmanifest is established.
Just as wherever there are threads, there is the cloth.
The threads are one thing and the cloth another; why? Because their identity is never observed.

In this way, the distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest is established: the *pradhāna* is distant and the manifest is near. He who perceives the manifest also perceives the *pradhāna*, because their non-identity is never observed. Furthermore, the unmanifest is proven by the fact that the effect possesses the qualities inherent in its cause.
In the world, whatever is the nature of the cause, such is the nature of the effect as well; for example, from black threads, only a black cloth arises.

In this way, since the mark consisting of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest is non-discriminative, an object of experience, common, conscious, and productive, it is established that the Unmanifest (avyakta), being of the same nature as that mark, is also of that same nature.
Because of the presence of the three qualities (traiguṇya), non-discrimination, and so forth, these properties are established in the manifest (vyakta); for their opposites are absent there.

Thus, because the effect consists of the qualities of its cause, it is established that the unmanifest (avyakta) also exists; this [objection] is false. In the world, that which is not perceived does not exist; yet the Pradhāna exists, though it is not perceived. [This is known] from the finite measure of differentiated objects, from their homogeneity, from their activity proceeding from a power, from the distinction between cause and effect, and from the non-differentiation of the manifold universe. (ISk 15)
The unmanifest exists as the cause; this is the relationship between action and its agent.

In the world, wherever there is a creator of differentiated things, their finite measure is observed, just as a potter produces a limited number of jars from a limited amount of clay. Likewise, the Great Principle (mahat) and the other signs, though vast, are finite in their differentiation; thus, the effect of Pradhāna is one.

Intellect, ego-sense, the five subtle elements, the eleven organs, and the five gross elements—because there is such a finite measure of these distinct manifestations, there exists the Pradhāna as their cause, which produces this manifested world that is itself finite.
If the Pradhāna did not exist, then this manifested world would likewise be infinite; however, because the manifestations are finite, the Pradhāna exists, from which the manifest has arisen.
Likewise, in this world, the establishment [of a cause] through "homogeneity" (samanvaya) is observed; for example, upon seeing a young brahmin boy observing his vows, one concludes:

"Surely his parents are brahmins. Similarly, having observed this tri-guṇa mark consisting of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, we establish that there must be a cause for it. Therefore, due to homogeneity, the Pradhāna exists.

Likewise, because activity occurs according to capacity: here, whatever is capable of a particular thing engages in that very object; for example, a potter, being capable of making a jar, makes only a jar, not a cloth or a chariot.
Thus, Pradhāna exists as the cause; why? Because of the distinction between cause and effect.
That which acts is the cause (*kāraṇa*); that which is acted upon is the effect (*kārya*).
The distinction between cause and effect is as follows: a jar is capable of holding curds, honey, water, and milk, whereas its cause, the lump of clay, is not so capable.
Just as a lump of clay produces a jar, but the jar does not likewise produce the lump of clay,
so too, having observed the mark consisting of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest,
it is inferred that there exists a distinct cause of which this manifest world is the differentiation.

Furthermore, [the existence of Pradhāna follows] from the non-differentiation of the manifold form (*vaiśvarūpya*). The "manifold" (*viśva*) is the world; its "form" (*rūpa*) is its manifestation. The state of being manifold is "manifoldness" (*vaiśvarūpya*); because of the non-differentiation of that, Pradhāna exists. For there is no mutual differentiation among the three worlds or among the five great elements, earth and so forth; the three worlds are included within the great elements.

Thus, earth, water, fire, air, and ether—these five great elements (mahābhūtas)—at the time of dissolution, proceed to a state of non-distinction (avibhāga) through the very same sequence as their creation, merging into the evolving subtle elements (tanmātras). The subtle elements and the eleven organs merge into the ego (ahaṃkāra); the ego merges into the intellect (buddhi); and the intellect merges into primordial matter (pradhāna). In this manner, the three worlds reach a state of non-distinction within primordial matter at the time of dissolution; from that non-distinction [proceeds the subsequent evolution].
As in the case of milk and curd, the unmanifest (avyakta) is the cause of the manifest and the unmanifest.
And for this reason:
there exists an unmanifest cause; it proceeds from the three qualities (guṇas) and from their combination.
By way of transformation, like water, [the elements] differ according to the specific basis of each respective quality.

There exists an unmanifest (avyakta) and well-known cause from which the manifest signs, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), proceed. It is "three-constituted" (triguṇataḥ), meaning it consists of the three qualities (guṇas): sattva, rajas, and tamas; what is meant by this is that the state of equilibrium among sattva, rajas, and tamas is Pradhāna.
Likewise, it is so called because of its "convergence" (samudayāt), just as the three streams of the Gaṅgā, having fallen upon the head of Rudra, produce a single stream.

Thus, the single unmanifest (avyakta), which consists of the three qualities (triguṇa), produces the manifest (vyakta); likewise, as threads combined produce a cloth, so the unmanifest produces the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest from the collection of the qualities. Therefore, the manifest world proceeds from both the three qualities and their combination. Since the manifest arises from the single Pradhāna, it ought to be of a single uniform nature.

This is not a fault; for, through transformation, like water, the three worlds arise from the single *pradhāna* and do not possess an identical state, because of the specific distinctions based on their respective substrates of the *guṇas*. Thus, gods are endowed with happiness, humans with suffering, and animals with delusion.

Although the manifest (*vyakta*) proceeds from the single *pradhāna*, it becomes like water through transformation due to the specific distinctions based on their respective substrates of the *guṇas*.
"Pratipratīti" means distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).

"Guṇāśrayaviśeṣam" refers to the specific substratum of the qualities (*guṇa*); having established itself in accordance with each such specific substratum of the qualities, the Manifest (*vyakta*) proceeds through transformation. For example, water falling from the sky as a single essence becomes divided by contact with various forms.

Thus, through these various modifications of those [qualities], the three worlds proceeding from a single primary cause do not possess a single nature: among the gods, *sattva* is predominant while *rajas* and *tamas* are subordinate; therefore, they are exceedingly happy. Among humans, *rajas* is predominant while *sattva* and *tamas* are subordinate; therefore, they are exceedingly miserable. Among animals, *tamas* is predominant.
Because they are born from the *sattva* and are indifferent, they are therefore utterly deluded.
(16) Thus, with these two verses, the existence of *pradhāna* is accepted.
Hereafter, he speaks for the purpose of establishing the existence of the *puruṣa*.
Because the composite is for the sake of another, because of the reversal of the three qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth,
because of superintendence, because there must be an experiencer, and because of activity for the sake of isolation (*kaivalya*), the Puruṣa exists.

Regarding what was stated—that liberation is attained through the discernment of the manifest (vyakta), the unmanifest (avyakta), and the Knower (vijñāna)—the unmanifest was understood immediately after the manifest by means of five reasons. Now, just as the unmanifest is subtle, the Puruṣa is also subtle; therefore, his existence is now established through inference. The Puruṣa exists. Why? Because composite things exist for the sake of another.
This aggregate consisting of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest is inferred to exist for the sake of the Puruṣa, because it is insentient, like a couch.

Just as a couch—which is an aggregate of individual parts such as the frame, the lotus-patterned coverlet, the legs, the cotton mattress, the bedspread, and the pillows—is for the sake of another and not for its own sake; for among the various components such as the frame and the lotus-patterned coverlet, there is no mutual purposeful activity whatsoever.

From this it is understood that there exists a person who lies upon the couch; for whose sake the couch exists, this body—a composite of the five great elements—exists for his sake. There exists a person for whom this body, which is an object of experience and has arisen as a composite of the principles beginning with Mahat, serves as an object of enjoyment.

For this reason as well, the Self exists, because of the reversal of the three qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. As was stated in the preceding verse—that [Prakṛti] consists of the three qualities, is non-discriminating, is an object, and so on—the Spirit (*puruṣa*) is the opposite of that which was described.

Furthermore, because of presiding (*adhiṣṭhāna*): just as here a chariot yoked with horses capable of leaping, galloping, and running proceeds only when presided over by a charioteer, so too does the body proceed through the presiding of the Self.
And so it is said in the *Ṣaṣṭhitantra*: "Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) proceeds when presided over by the Person (*puruṣa*);
therefore, the Self exists because there must be an experiencer.

Just as the experience of food that is prepared and enriched with the six tastes—sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent—is established, so too, because the indicative mark consisting of the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest lacks an experiencer, that Self exists to whom this [aggregate] belongs."
The body is that which is to be experienced.

Furthermore, from the fact that activity proceeds for the sake of isolation (*kaivalya*), it is inferred that the Self exists; for "isolation" is the state of being alone (*kevalasya bhāvaḥ*), and from that activity directed toward one's own isolation—activity which both the learned and the ignorant alike undertake—it is concluded that the Self exists.
He desires the exhaustion of the continuity of saṃsāra.
Thus, by these reasons, there exists a self distinct from the body.

Now, as to whether that [self] is a single presiding entity over all bodies—like a thread running through a string of jewels—or whether there are many selves, each presiding over its respective body, it is said in response:
The plurality of Puruṣas is established by the specific determination of birth, death, and the instruments [of perception], by their non-simultaneous activity,
and also by the diversity of the three guṇas.
Birth, death, and the instruments [of perception] constitute "birth-death-instruments"; the meaning is that there is a specific determination for each of these.
If the self were indeed one and the same, then when one is born, all would be born; when one dies, all would die;
and when one suffers a deficiency of the instruments—characterized by deafness, blindness, muteness, lameness, or being crippled—all would likewise suffer such deficiencies.

There would otherwise be deafness, blindness, mutilation, and lameness; yet this is not the case. Therefore, because there is a specific determination of the instruments (karaṇas) for birth and death, the plurality of Puruṣas is established. Furthermore, it is because of their non-simultaneous activity: activity does not occur simultaneously at one and the same time, since there is non-simultaneity with respect to dharma and the other [guṇas].
Activity is observed: some are engaged in dharma, others in adharma; some are engaged in dispassion, others in knowledge.
Therefore, because their activities are not simultaneous, it is established that there are many [purusas].
Furthermore, from the non-reversal of the three gunas—that is, from the non-reversal of the state of the three gunas—the multiplicity of purusas is established.
Just as in the case of birth in general, one is of the nature of *sattva* and happy, another is of the nature of *rajas* and suffering,
and another is of the nature of *tamas* and deluded.
Thus, through the reversal of the three qualities (guṇas), plurality is established.
[Kārikā 18] It is said that the Puruṣa is not an agent. And because of this contrast, the witnesshood of this Puruṣa is established.
Isolation, neutrality, the state of being a witness, and the state of being a non-agent.

And from that inversion, and from that aforementioned inversion of the three *guṇas*, [the following follows]: because of the inversion stated regarding the qualities—namely, that the *puruṣa* is devoid of *guṇas*, discriminative, the enjoyer, and so forth—it is established that the *puruṣa* is the witness (*sākṣitva*) while *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* function as the agents; this is the same *puruṣa* who was the subject of discussion regarding plurality.
The qualities alone act as agents; the witness neither acts nor desists from acting.
Furthermore, *kaivalya* means the state of being solitary (*kevalabhāva*), that is to say, isolation (*anyatva*).
It is solitary in relation to the three qualities.
Furthermore, neutrality (*mādhyasthya*) is the state of being neutral (*madhyasthabhāva*), like that of a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*).

Just as a certain wandering mendicant remains merely a neutral person when villagers are engaged in agricultural labor, so too the *puruṣa* does not engage while the *guṇas* are active. Therefore, because he is neutral due to his state of being a non-agent, the *puruṣa* is a witness; thus, the *puruṣa* is a non-agent with respect to them.
Regarding "of actions": the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—operate in the capacity of both the action and the agent, and not the *puruṣa* alone;

thus, the existence of the *puruṣa* is established. Since the *puruṣa* is the agent, how does he exercise determination (*adhyavasāya*)? [He thinks: "I shall perform dharma; I shall not perform adharma. Therefore, he is the agent. And yet, the *puruṣa* is not the agent; thus, in both respects...
"There would be a fault"—this is what is said.
Therefore it is stated:
"Therefore, through union with that [Puruṣa], the unconscious *liṅga* appears as if it were conscious."
Even though the qualities are the agents, the indifferent Self likewise appears as the agent.

In this world, the Person (puruṣa) is consciousness itself; therefore, the subtle body (liṅga), consisting of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, being joined with that which is the reflection of consciousness, becomes as if it were conscious.

Just as in the world a jar becomes cold when conjoined with cold and hot when conjoined with heat, so too the subtle body, consisting of the Great Principle and the rest, through its conjunction with that [consciousness]—that is, through conjunction with the Person—becomes as if it were conscious. Therefore, it is the guṇas that perform the act of determination (adhyavasāya), not the Person.

Although in the world it is said that "the person is the agent," "he goes," and so forth, nevertheless, the person is not an agent. How so? While the qualities (guṇas) are the agents, the indifferent person appears as if he were the agent; yet, even while the qualities are acting, the indifferent person is merely like an agent, not truly an agent. Here there is an illustration: just as a non-thief who is seized along with thieves is understood to be a thief, so too the three qualities are the agents, and the person, though not an agent, becomes as if an agent through association with them.
[This occurs] due to the conjunction with the agent.

Thus, the distinction between the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower has been explained; through this distinction, the attainment of liberation occurs. // 20 // Now, what is said to be the cause of the conjunction of these two—the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa?

For the purpose of the Spirit's perception and likewise for the purpose of the Primal Matter's isolation, there is a conjunction of both, like that of the lame and the blind; from this conjunction, creation proceeds.

The conjunction of the *puruṣa* with *pradhāna* is for the purpose of perception; by means of this, the *puruṣa* perceives *prakṛti*, from the effects beginning with the *mahat* down to the gross elements. For the sake of liberation (*kaivalya*), there is likewise a conjunction of *pradhāna* with the *puruṣa*. This conjunction of both should be understood as being like that of the lame man and the blind man: just as one is lame and the other is blind, and these two, traveling together with great effort through a forest, are abandoned by their kinsmen due to an attack by robbers upon their caravan.

By chance, they wandered about and again came together through their own movements; because of the mutual trust established by their own words, their union was for the purpose of traveling and seeing. Thus, the blind man was mounted upon the shoulders of the lame man;
in this way, the blind man went along the path shown by the lame man mounted on his body, while the lame man remained mounted upon the shoulders of the blind man.
Thus, the Puruṣa possesses the power of vision but lacks the power of action, like a lame man; the Pradhāna possesses the power of action but lacks the power of vision, like a blind man.

Just as this division between the lame man and the blind man will occur once their purpose is fulfilled upon reaching their desired destination, so too the Pradhāna ceases its activity after effecting the liberation of the Puruṣa, and the Puruṣa likewise attains isolation (kaivalya) having seen the Pradhāna.
When those two have accomplished their purpose, a separation will occur between them.
Furthermore, "created by that" means the creation (sarga) is produced by that conjunction; it is a creation brought about by that union.
Just as the birth of a son occurs from the union of a woman and a man, so too the production of creation arises from the conjunction of Pradhāna and Puruṣa. (21)
Now, for the purpose of showing all the divisions, he says:

"From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); from that, the group of sixteen; and from five of that group of sixteen, the five gross elements (bhūta). (ISk 22)

*Prakṛti*, *pradhāna*, *brahman*, *avyakta*, *bahudhānaka*, and *māyā* are synonyms. From this unmanifest *prakṛti*, which is devoid of marks (*aliṅga*), the Great One (*mahat*) is produced; the Great One is produced through the synonyms of intellect (*buddhi*), *āsurī*, *mati*, *khyāti*, *jñāna*, and *prajñā*. And from that Great One, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is produced—the ego-sense which is the source of the elements (*bhūtādi*), the modified (*vaikṛta*), and the radiant (*taijasa*).

‘Abhimāna’ (ego) is a synonym for it; therefore, from that ego, the group of sixteen arises. From that ego, the sixteenfold quality is produced in the form of sixteen constituents. It is as follows: the five subtle elements—namely, the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell.
These are designated by the subtle synonyms of the *tanmātras*.

From that [ahaṃkāra], the eleven organs arise: the five sense organs, namely the ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose; the five organs of action, namely speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; and the eleventh, the mind (*manas*), which partakes of the nature of both. This group of sixteen is produced from ahaṃkāra.

Furthermore, from the five [subtle elements], the five gross elements arise; that is, from the group of sixteen, specifically from the five *tanmātras*, the five great elements (*mahābhūtas*) are produced.

As it has been stated: from the *tanmātra* of sound arises space (*ākāśa*); from the *tanmātra* of touch, air (*vāyu*); from the *tanmātra* of form, fire (*tejas*); from the *tanmātra* of taste, water (*āpas*); and from the *tanmātra* of smell, earth (*pṛthivī*). Thus, from the five subtle atoms (*paramāṇus*), the five great elements are produced. (22)

Regarding what was stated—that liberation results from the discernment of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower—the manifest, consisting of twenty-three divisions beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the gross elements, has been explained;

the unmanifest has also been explained by such reasons as "because of the limitation of the divisions" and so forth; and the Puruṣa has likewise been explained by such reasons as "because the composite is for the sake of another" and so forth.
Thus, the state or existence (*bhāva*)—the reality (*tattva*)—of one who knows these twenty-five principles that pervade the three worlds is as it has been described.

One who knows the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), regardless of which stage of life (*āśrama*) he is devoted to—whether he has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot—is liberated; there is no doubt about this.

These [principles] are as follows: primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the spirit (*puruṣa*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the eleven sense organs (*indriya*), and the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*). These are the twenty-five principles.

In that regard, it has been stated that the Great Principle (mahat) arises from primordial nature (prakṛti). What is the characteristic of that Great Principle? To this, he says: "Intellect (buddhi) is determination; its forms are virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and power.
This is its sattvic form; the tamasic form is the opposite of this. (ISk 23)

Ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) is the defining characteristic of intellect (*buddhi*). Ascertainment means the act of ascertaining; just as a sprout exists potentially within a seed, so too this ascertainment—such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth"—is that which is defined as intellect. And that intellect is eightfold, due to the distinctions between its *sāttvika* and *tāmasa* forms.
In that regard, the sattvic form of the intellect (buddhi) is fourfold: virtue (dharma), knowledge (jñāna), dispassion (vairāgya), and sovereignty (aiśvarya).
Among these, virtue is characterized by compassion, charity, restraint (yama), and observance (niyama). Regarding this, the restraints and observances are set forth in the Pātañjala [Yoga Sūtra]:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the restraints; purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances.
Knowledge (*jñāna*), illumination (*prakāśa*), comprehension (*avagama*), and manifestation (*bhāna*) are synonyms. That [knowledge] is of two kinds: external and internal.

Among these, the "external" consists of the Vedas along with their six limbs—phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual procedure (*kalpa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), etymology (*nirukta*), prosody (*chandas*), and astronomy (*jyotiṣa*)—as well as the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Dharmaśāstras.

Internal knowledge is the knowledge of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*: that this *prakṛti* is the state of equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; and that this *puruṣa* is established as being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), all-pervading (*vyāpin*), and conscious (*cetana*). In this context, external knowledge refers to worldly standing and affection for the world; internal knowledge refers to liberation. Detachment (*vairāgya*) is also twofold: external and internal.
External detachment arises from seeing the defects in objects of perception—namely, their acquisition, preservation, decay, attachment, and destruction.

Internal detachment, however, arises for one who is already detached from these and seeks liberation, when they perceive even the primary principle (*pradhāna*) as being like a dream or a magical illusion; this is internal detachment.

Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is the state of being a lord, and it consists of eight qualities: *aṇimā* (minuteness), *mahimā* (magnitude), *garimā* (heaviness), *laghimā* (lightness), *prāpti* (attainment), *prākāmya* (efficacy), *īśitva* (lordship), *vaśitva* (control), and *yatrakāmāvasāyitva* (the power to determine things according to one's will).
Aṇimā is the state of being minute; having become subtle, one moves about in the world. Mahimā is the state of being great; having become vast, one moves about.
Laghimā is the state of being light; by virtue of being lighter than even a portion of a lotus fiber or cotton, one can stand even upon the tips of flower filaments.

Attainment (*prāpti*) means that wherever one may be situated, one obtains the desired object. Irresistible will (*prākāmya*) means that one brings about exactly whatever one desires according to one's wish. Sovereignty (*īśitva*) means that by virtue of lordship, one rules even over the three worlds.
Mastery means that everything comes under one's control.

Regarding the power of determining one's own desires (*kāmāvasāyitva*), from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, wherever there is a desire, there one performs standing, sitting, and moving according to one's own will.

These four are the *sāttvika* forms of the intellect (*buddhi*). When *rajas* and *tamas* are overcome by *sattva*, then the person attains the qualities of the intellect, such as virtue (*dharma*) and the rest.

Furthermore, that which is contrary to this [sāttvika state] is tāmasa; it is the opposite of dharma and the other [qualities]. Tāmasa consists of the form of intellect (buddhi) and is the opposite of dharma, namely: adharma, ignorance (ajñāna), non-detachment (avairāgya), and lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya). Thus, through these sāttvika and tāmasa forms, the eightfold intellect is produced from the unmanifest (avyakta) composed of the three guṇas.
Having thus described the definition of the intellect, the definition of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is now stated.
From that ego (ahaṃkāra), which is characterized by self-conceit (abhimāna), a twofold creation proceeds:
the elevenfold group of the senses and the fivefold group of subtle elements (tanmātra).

The group of eleven consists of the eleven organs; likewise, the group of five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) is endowed with five characteristics—that is, it is endowed with the characteristics of the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell.
To the question "From what characteristic does creation proceed?", he says:
"The sattvic group of eleven proceeds from the *vaikṛta* ego."
From the *bhūtādi* arises the subtle element (*tanmātra*), which is *tāmasa*; from the *taijasa* arise both.

When *rajas* and *tamas* are overcome by *sattva* within the *ahaṃkāra*, then that *ahaṃkāra* is *sāttvika*. Its name was designated as "the modified" (*vaikṛta*) by the ancient teachers. From that modified *ahaṃkāra*, the group of eleven organs arises.
Therefore, the organs are *sāttvika* and pure, capable of their respective objects; hence it is said that the group of eleven is *sāttvika*.
Furthermore, regarding the "origin of the elements" (*bhūtādi*): when the *sattva* and *rajas* qualities are overwhelmed by *tamas* within the *ahaṃkāra*, that *ahaṃkāra* is called *tāmasa*.

Its name, established by former teachers, is *bhūtādi*. From this *bhūtādi-ahaṃkāra*, the group of five *tanmātras* arises; because it is the source of the elements and is abundant in *tamas*, it is described as *tāmasa*.

Therefore, from the *bhūtādi* [ego], the group of five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) arises. Furthermore, from the *taijasa* [ego], both arise. When *sattva* and *tamas* are overwhelmed by *rajas*, that ego receives the designation "taijasa"; from that *taijasa*, both are produced. "Both" refers to the group of eleven [senses] and the group of five subtle elements.

This *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which is *vaikṛtika*, having become modified (*vaikṛta*), produces the eleven organs by taking the *taijasa* ego as its assistant; for the *sāttvika* ego is inactive and, when joined with the *taijasa*, becomes capable of producing the organs. Likewise, the *tāmasa* ego, known as *bhūtādi*, being inactive, produces the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) when joined with the active *taijasa* ego.
It was stated by him that "both [arise] from the *taijasa*"; thus, by means of the *taijasa* ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the eleven organs and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are produced.
Regarding the group of eleven that is said to arise from the modified (*vaikṛta*) or *sāttvika* ego, he states what its designation is:
The sense organs are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin;
they say that speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ are the organs of action.
The faculties beginning with the eye and ending with the skin are called the cognitive faculties (*buddhīndriya*).

"Sparśana" refers to that by which one touches; it is established as a term denoting the tactile faculty (*tvagindriya*), and thus this is recited as "the tactile organs" (*sparśanakāni*). They perceive—that is, they cognize—the five objects: sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

There are five sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*). They call the speech organ, hands, feet, anus, and genitals the organs of action (*karmendriya*), because they perform actions; thus they are called *karmendriya*. Among them, speech speaks; the two hands perform various activities; the two feet perform going and coming; the anus performs excretion; and the genitals perform pleasure through the production of offspring. (26)
Thus, the ten sense organs have been explained through the division of the cognitive and active organs. Now, it is stated what the nature and essential form of the mind—the eleventh—are:
"In this context, the mind partakes of the nature of both; it is the faculty of volition and is also a sense organ due to its common characteristics.
Its diversity arises from the specific transformations of the *guṇas* and from the distinction between the external [objects]. (ISk 27)

In this group of faculties, the mind (*manas*) is of a dual nature: it is like a faculty of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) among the faculties of cognition, and like a faculty of action (*karmendriya*) among the faculties of action.
Why? Because it initiates the activity of the faculties of cognition and that of the faculties of action; therefore, the mind is of a dual nature.
It is called "the volitional" (*saṃkalpaka*) because it forms intentions (*saṃkalpa*).

Furthermore, because of their commonality—that is, because they possess the same attributes—the sense organs (*buddhīndriyas*) and the organs of action (*karmendriyas*), arising together with the mind from the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṃkāra*), share a similarity with the mind; therefore, due to this commonality, the mind is also an organ.
Thus, these eleven organs are produced from the *vaikṛta* (transformative) *sāttvika* ego.
In that regard, what is the function of the mind?
Its function is volition (*saṃkalpa*).
The functions of the sense organs of cognition are sound and the rest; the functions of the organs of action are speech and the rest. Now, these sense organs are distinct.

Are those [faculties] which grasp distinct objects created by Īśvara or by *svabhāva*? Since the *pradhāna*, *buddhi*, and *ahaṃkāra* are insentient (*acetana*) and the *puruṣa* is also not an agent, he says in response:
"In this system of the Sāṃkhyas, there exists a certain cause called *svabhāva*."
To this it is replied: the diversity and the external distinctions arise from the specific transformations of the *guṇas*.

These eleven organs—the five [objects] of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; the five functions of the [five active organs], namely speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and procreating; and volition, which belongs to the mind—these are the objects of the distinct organs themselves, resulting from the specific transformations of the *guṇas*.
The transformation of the *guṇas* is "guṇapariṇāma"; from its particularity arises the diversity of the sense organs as well as the distinctions among external objects.

Now, this diversity is not produced by Īśvara, nor by the *ahaṃkāra*, nor by the *buddhi*, nor by *pradhāna*, nor by the *puruṣa*; rather, it is produced by the transformation of the *guṇas* through their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*). Since the *guṇas* are insentient, they do not act [of their own accord]; yet they certainly do act. How so? It will be stated right here: "Just as the flow of milk occurs for the sake of the growth of the calf, even though it is insentient, so too does [the activity of nature] proceed for the sake of the liberation of the *puruṣa*."
Such is the activity of Pradhāna.

In this way, the insentient guṇas proceed as the eleven organs; the specific locations are also produced by that very [Pradhāna], whereby the eye is situated in a high place for the purpose of seeing the world, and likewise the nose, the ear, and the tongue are situated in their respective places for the apprehension of their own objects.

In the same way, the organs of action (karmendriya) also, being situated in their respective locations, are capable of their own specific functions by virtue of the particular transformation of the qualities (guṇa-pariṇāma-viśeṣa) inherent in their own nature; they do not exist for the sake of those objects [of the senses]. For it is said in another treatise: "The qualities operate within the qualities; whatever is the operation of the qualities, its object is the qualities themselves. This means that external objects are to be understood as being produced solely by the qualities. Thus, primordial matter (pradhāna) is the cause of this [manifestation]. // 27 //
Now, it is stated which function belongs to which sense organ:

the function of the five [sensory organs] with respect to sound and the other objects is held to be mere observation; while speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure are the functions of the five [action organs].
