The word *mātra* (only) has the sense of specification; it serves to exclude what is not specified, just as when one says "only alms are obtained, no other special item," so too the eye [perceives] only form (*rūpa*) and not taste (*rasa*) and the rest. The same applies to the remaining [faculties]: namely, form for the eye, taste for the tongue, odor for the nose, sound for the ear, and touch for the skin.

Thus, the function of these organs of perception has been described; now the function of the organs of action is stated. The meaning is that speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure are the functions of the five organs of action. The connection is as follows: speaking is the function of speech, grasping of the hands, moving of the feet, the excretion of digested waste from the food consumed by the anus, and sexual pleasure (as well as procreation) of the generative organ—these are their respective objects and functions. Now, the functions of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*) are being explained.
The specific functioning of the triad [of the organs] is unique to each;
however, the common functioning of the instruments consists of the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa.

That which has the nature of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is "possessing its own characteristics" (*svālakṣaṇyā*). As for the definition stated that "determination (*adhyavasāya*) is intellect (*buddhi*)," that very [intellect] is the function of intellect.
Likewise, as for the definition that "egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is self-conceit (*abhimāna*"), it is characterized by self-conceit and its function is self-conceit.

The definition of the mind (*manas*) has been stated as "that which forms volitional constructs" (*saṃkalpaka*); therefore, volitional construction itself is the specific function (*vṛtti*) of the mind.

Regarding the triad of intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind, the previously mentioned functions characterized by their own specific traits (*svālakṣaṇya*)—namely, the functions of the organs of perception (*buddhīndriya*)—are also non-common (*asāmānya*).
Now, the common (*sāmānya*) function is being described.

The "general function of the instruments" (*sāmānyakaraṇavṛtti*) refers to the general activity of the instruments. It consists of the five vital airs (*vāyu*), namely *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, *udāna*, and *vyāna*. These five airs constitute the common function of all the sense organs, because the air called *prāṇa*—which has its range within the mouth and nose—possesses a vibration as its action, and that is the common function of even the thirteenfold group [of instruments]. For it is when *prāṇa* exists that the instruments obtain their very existence.
The *prāṇa* also causes the movement of everything, like a bird with five feathers;
because it breathes forth (*prāṇana*), it is called *prāṇa*. Likewise, because it carries away (*apanayana*), it is the *apāna*; the pulsation therein is also a general function of the sense organ.

Likewise, the *samāna* wind, which abides in the middle of the body and is so called because it leads [the food] equally—that is, because it carries it evenly—is present there; its vibration is the common function (*sāmānya-vṛtti*) of the instruments (*karaṇa*).

Similarly, the *udāna* wind, so called because of its upward movement, excellence, or leading upwards, has as its range the area from the navel region to the head; the vibration therein is the common function of all the sense organs.

Furthermore, that by which the pervasion of the body and the internal differentiation are effected is the *vyāna*, which, like space, pervades the body; the vibration therein is the common function of the entire network of instruments.

Thus, these five vital airs (vāyus) have been explained as the "common function of the instruments" (sāmānyakaraṇavṛtti); the meaning is that they constitute the common functioning of all thirteen types of instruments. But the functioning of the fourfold [group] is both simultaneous and successive; likewise, it is taught for the unseen [object]. However, with respect to the seen, the functioning of the triad is preceded by that [fourfold group]. (ISk 30)

When there is a simultaneous connection of the fourfold group—consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), and the mind (*manas*)—with each individual sense organ, a fourfold state arises.

Regarding the determination of an object within the range of perception, the simultaneous functioning of the four—the intellect, ego-consciousness, the mind, and the eye—perceives the form at one and the same time, [cognizing]: "This is a post."
The intellect (*buddhi*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the mind (*manas*), and the tongue (*jihvā*) perceive taste simultaneously.
The intellect, the ego-sense, the mind, and the nose (*ghrāṇa*) perceive odor simultaneously;
the same applies to the skin (*tvak*) and the ear (*śrotra*).
Furthermore, its occurrence is specified as being gradual; that is, the occurrence of this fourfold [process] is gradual.

For example, when someone walking on a path sees something from afar and, upon the doubt arising whether it is a post or a person, he perceives a creeper growing upon it or a bird [therein] as a sign. Then, regarding that doubt conceived by his mind, [the perception serves as] the exclusion.

The intellect (*buddhi*) arises [as the thought], "This is a post," and from that comes the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) for the sake of ascertainment, "It is indeed a post. Thus, the sequential functioning of the intellect, ego-sense, mind, and eye is observed with respect to a visible object; as it is with regard to form (*rūpa*), so it should be understood regarding sound and the other objects when they are perceived within the domain of the seen. Furthermore, even with respect to the unseen—the future, the past, and [other] times—the functioning of the triad of intellect, ego-sense, and mind is preceded by that [perception].

In the case of form, the operation of the triad [of intellect, ego, and mind] is preceded by the eye; in the case of touch, it is preceded by the skin; in the case of smell, by the nose; in the case of taste, by the tongue; and in the case of sound, by the ear. Regarding the future—that is, in the time yet to come—and the past, the operation of the intellect, ego, and mind occurs sequentially. In the present, however, it occurs both simultaneously and sequentially. // 30 //
Furthermore:
each [organ] adopts its own respective mode of activity, which is caused by the mutual intention [of the others].
The purpose of the Puruṣa alone is the cause; no instrument is set in motion by anything else.

"Each its own"—this repetition (*vīpsā*) refers to the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*). Each attains its respective function, which is caused by mutual intention (*ākūta*), in the form of an intent, a regard, and an agitation, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the *puruṣa*. The ego-sense and the others [attain their functions] after the intellect has understood the intention of the ego-sense; as to why this is so, the answer is that the purpose of the *puruṣa* alone is the cause. The activity of the *guṇas* is for the sake of the thought, "The purpose of the *puruṣa* must be accomplished. Therefore, these [function].
The instruments manifest the purpose of the Puruṣa; how do they operate of their own accord? No one causes the instrument to act;
rather, the sole purpose of the Puruṣa is what causes it to act—this is the meaning of the statement. The instrument is not caused or prompted by anyone, such as a Lord (Īśvara) or a person (Puruṣa).
It is now stated how many kinds of these [instruments], beginning with the intellect (buddhi), there are:
The instrument is of thirteen kinds; it performs the functions of grasping, maintaining, and illuminating.
And its object is tenfold: that which is to be grasped, maintained, and illuminated.

The instrument (*karaṇa*) should be understood as being thirteenfold: the five sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), such as the eye and so forth; and the five organs of action (*karmendriya*), such as speech and so forth. As to what that thirteenfold instrument does, it is said: "It performs seizing (*āharaṇa*), retaining (*dhāraṇa*), and illuminating (*prakāśa*). Among these, the organs of action perform seizing and retaining, while the organs of cognition perform illuminating.
What is the nature of its effect? That is now explained: its effect is tenfold. The effect of that instrument is that which is to be accomplished; thus it is tenfold, consisting of ten types:
namely, those called sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, and those called speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and sexual pleasure. This is the tenfold effect.

The organs of action take up and sustain that which has been illuminated by the organs of cognition. // 32 // The internal organ is threefold; the external is tenfold, being designated as the objects of the [three internal organs].
The external organ functions in the present time, while the internal organ functions across the three times. // 33 //
The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is threefold, consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*), due to the distinction between the "great one" (*mahat*) and the others.

The external organ is tenfold: five organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) and five organs of action (*karmendriya*). This tenfold external instrument belongs to that internal organ; it is called the "object" (*viṣaya*), and it is the object of enjoyment for the intellect, ego, and mind, pertaining to the present time.

The ear hears only a present sound, not one that is past nor one that is yet to come; the eye likewise sees a present form, not one that is past nor one that is future; the skin [feels] a present touch, the tongue a present taste, and the nose a present odor—not those that are past or future.

Thus, the organs of action: speech utters a present sound, not one past or future; the hands grasp a present jar, not one past or future; and the anus and the generative organ perform their functions of excretion and pleasure in the present, not in the past or future. Thus, the external instruments have been described as pertaining to the present time. The internal instruments—the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*)—have objects belonging to all three times. The intellect perceives a present jar.
"Regarding the past and the future":
the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense) forms an identification (*abhimāna*) with the present, as well as with the past and the future.

Likewise, the *manas* (mind) forms volitions (*saṃkalpa*) regarding the present, as well as the past and the future. Thus, the internal instrument (*karaṇa*) operates across the three periods of time. // 33 //
Now it is stated which of the sense organs perceive their objects with distinctions and which perceive them without distinctions:
"Among those, the five organs of cognition have as their objects both the specific and the non-specific;
speech has sound as its object, while the remaining [organs] also have fivefold objects. (ISk 34)

Those sense organs (buddhīndriyas) perceive their objects with specific qualities; they manifest for humans objects with specific qualities—namely sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, joined with the objects of pleasure, pain, and delusion—and for the gods, they manifest objects devoid of specific qualities. Likewise, among the organs of action (karmendriyas), speech has sound as its object for the gods and for humans.

And since speech utters and articulates verses and the like, therefore the vocal faculty of gods and humans is equal. Furthermore, the remaining faculties—those distinct from speech, namely those known as the hand, foot, anus, and genitals—possess five objects; these five objects are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. The hand possesses [the capacity for] these five objects, such as sound and so forth, and the foot moves upon the ground characterized by these five objects, such as sound and the rest.
The organ of excretion, characterized by five functions, performs evacuation; likewise, the organ of generation, possessing five attributes, brings joy through the emission of semen.

// 34 // Since the intellect, together with the internal organs, penetrates all objects of experience, therefore the threefold instrument is the gatekeeper, while the remaining ones are the gates. // 35 //

The intellect (*buddhi*), together with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—meaning accompanied by the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and the mind (*manas*)—penetrates and grasps every object; it grasps sound and the other sense-objects throughout all three periods of time. Therefore, this threefold instrument is the "gatekeeper," while the remaining instruments are the "gates"—this is the completion of the sentence. // 35 //
Furthermore:
These specific qualities, which are like lamps and distinct from one another,
having illuminated the entire purpose of the Puruṣa, present it to the intellect.

Those instruments which have been described are these specific qualities (*guṇaviśeṣāḥ*). What are they like? They are "like lamps" (*pradīpakalpāḥ*), meaning they illuminate their objects like lamps; they are mutually distinct, dissimilar, and have different objects—this is the meaning. That is to say, they have the qualities (*guṇa*) as their objects. These specific qualities are born from the qualities (*guṇebhyo jātāḥ*).

The sense organs, the organs of action, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and the mind—all these, having illuminated their respective objects for the sake of the Puruṣa, present them to the intellect (buddhi); the meaning is that they place them within the intellect. For it is from the intellect that the Puruṣa perceives all objects, such as pleasure and so forth. (36)
And this is another point:
since the intellect accomplishes everything for the sake of the person's experience,
it is that very intellect which distinguishes the subtle difference between the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa.

Since the intellect (*buddhi*), together with the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), accomplishes— that is, brings about— all experience pertaining to every sense-organ throughout all three periods of time, by means of the gateways of the cognitive and active organs among gods, humans, and animals; therefore, it alone distinguishes— that is, effects the separation of the spheres of— Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) and the Spirit (*puruṣa*), meaning it establishes the difference between Primal Matter and the Spirit.
"Subtle" means unattainable by those who have not undertaken the practice of austerity; this is *prakṛti*, the state of equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*;

this is *buddhi*; this is *ahaṃkāra*; these are the five *tanmātras*, the eleven organs, and the five gross elements; and this is the *puruṣa*, distinct from these—all this is what the intellect (*buddhi*) makes known, through the attainment of which liberation (*apavarga*) occurs. // 37 //
It was previously stated that [the senses] have as their objects the *viśeṣas* and *aviśeṣas*; he now demonstrates what those objects are:
"The *tanmātras* are the *aviśeṣas*; from these five, the five gross elements arise. These are known as the *viśeṣas*, being calm, terrible, and delusive. (ISk 38)

Those five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) which arise from the ego (*ahaṃkāra*)—namely, the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell—are called "non-specific" (*aviśeṣa*). These are the objects of the gods, characterized by pleasure and devoid of pain and delusion. From these five subtle elements, the five gross elements (*mahābhūtas*) arise, known as earth, water, fire, air, and space.
These are known as the specific manifestations (*viśeṣa*).
From the subtle element of smell arises earth; from the subtle element of taste, water; from the subtle element of form, fire; from the subtle element of touch, air;
and from the subtle element of sound, ether. Thus produced are these great elements (*mahābhūta*); these specific manifestations are the objects of human experience.

It is peaceful, characterized by happiness; it is terrible, characterized by suffering; it is deluded, producing confusion. Just as space becomes peaceful and pleasant for someone who has emerged from an enclosed house or similar place because there is no obstruction, yet that very same space becomes painful and terrible for one overcome by cold, heat, wind, and rain, and becomes deluded for one traveling on a path who has strayed from the forest track due to disorientation regarding the directions.
In this way, wind is pleasant to one afflicted by heat, but terrible to one afflicted by cold; when it blows excessively, mixed with dust and gravel, it is delusive.
The same should be understood regarding fire and the other elements.
Now, there are other distinctions.
The subtle [beings], those born of parents, and those that are abundant—these are the three kinds of distinctions.
Among them, the subtle ones are constant, while those born of parents cease.

The subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are subtle; that which is comprised of these subtle elements is the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*), which is the *liṅga* (sign/vehicle) consisting of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the others. It remains eternally and transmigrates. Likewise, there are the [elements] born of mother and father which serve to nourish the gross body; at the time of conception, through the union of the parents, by means of the mixture of blood and semen within the womb, they effect the growth of the subtle body—that is the subtle body.
Furthermore, it is nourished by the various tastes of what the mother eats and drinks through the umbilical cord; likewise, the body initiated [in this way],

together with the subtle elements and those derived from the parents, along with the three kinds of specific great elements (mahābhūtas), consists of six parts— back, belly, shanks, hips, chest, and head— and is composed of the five elements, being filled with blood, flesh, sinews, semen, bone, and marrow, and [pervaded by] space.

Through the granting of space, it becomes wind; through growth, fire; through cooking (maturation), water; through cohesion, earth; and through support, it emerges from the mother's womb endowed with all its parts.
Thus, these are the three kinds of specific qualities.

To this he says: Which are eternal, and which are non-eternal? The subtle ones among them are fixed; those designated as *tanmātra*s (subtle elements) are fixed and eternal. The body commenced by them migrates, under the influence of karma, through the classes of domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and stationary beings; and under the influence of merit (*dharma*), it migrates through the worlds of Indra and others. Thus, this fixed subtle body migrates until knowledge arises.

When knowledge has arisen, the wise man, having abandoned the body, goes to liberation; therefore, these subtle and eternal specificities [the *tanmātras*] remain, while those born of mother and father cease. Having abandoned that subtle body, at the very moment of the abandonment of life right here, those born of mother and father cease;
at the time of death, the body born of mother and father, having ceased right here, dissolves into earth and the other elements according to their true nature. (39)
And as for how the subtle [body] transmigrates, he says:

"The *liṅga* (the subtle body), which has arisen previously, is unattached, determinate, and extends from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the subtle elements; devoid of experience, it transmigrates, permeated by latent dispositions (*bhāva*). (ISk 40)
When the worlds have not yet arisen during the creation from *pradhāna* and so forth, then the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) has arisen.

Furthermore, it is unattached—that is, not joined—and because of its subtlety, it moves unhindered through the states of animals, gods, and humans; being unattached, it travels with unimpeded movement even among mountains and other such obstacles.

It transmigrates constantly as long as knowledge has not arisen; and that [subtle body] consists of the principles beginning with the Great One (*mahat*) and ending with the subtle elements. "The Great One" (*mahān*) is at the beginning...

That subtle body—consisting of the Great Principle (mahat), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), mind (manas), and the five subtle elements (tanmātra) extending to the level of the subtle elements—wanders through all three worlds like an ant carrying a blade of grass.

Although it is devoid of experience and lacks enjoyment, this subtle body becomes capable of experiencing objects through the acquisition of the properties of action by means of the external accumulation born of father and mother. This is the meaning.
It is perfumed by dispositions (*bhāva*); we shall later explain the dispositions, such as *dharma* and the rest, by which it is perfumed—that is, colored—the *liṅga*.

At the time of dissolution, the subtle body, beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ending with the subtle elements, together with its instruments, merges into *pradhāna*. Being then devoid of transmigration, it remains there until the time of creation.
Bound by the fetter of the delusion of *prakṛti*, it is incapable of the activities of transmigration and so forth.
Furthermore, at the time of creation, it transmigrates; therefore, the subtle body (*liṅga*) [exists].
When it is asked for what purpose the thirteenfold instrument (*karaṇa*) transmigrates, he says in response:
"Just as a painting cannot exist without a support, or as a shadow cannot exist without a post or other such objects," [so too the subtle body transmigrates].
In the same way, the subtle body (liṅga) does not remain without a support in the absence of the specific qualities (viśeṣas).

Just as a painting does not exist without a support such as a wall, and as a shadow does not exist without posts, stakes, and so forth— by the inclusion of the phrase "and so forth," it is meant that water cannot exist without coldness,

nor coldness without water; fire without heat, wind without touch, space without room, and earth without smell— in the same way, by this illustration and logical principle, there can be no gross elements without their specific qualities, nor the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) without their non-specific [subtle] counterparts.
It does not remain stationary.

Now, the specific elements are described: the body consists of the five elements; apart from the specific body, where is the location of the subtle body (*liṅga*)? When it abandons one body, it takes up another; the subtle body (*liṅga*), being without support and devoid of a physical substrate, consists of thirteen components.
The meaning is that it is the instrument of manifestation.
(41) For what purpose is this stated? It is for the sake of the goal of the Puruṣa, through the sequence of causes and their effects.
Due to its connection with the pervasive power of primordial nature (prakṛti), the subtle body (liṅga) assumes various forms like an actor.

"The primary cause (pradhāna) operates because the purpose of the Spirit (puruṣārtha) must be accomplished; and that purpose is twofold: characterized by the perception of sound and so forth, and characterized by the perception of the distinction between the Guṇas and the Spirit.

The perception of sound and so forth consists in the attainment of enjoyments such as fragrance in the worlds beginning with Brahmaloka; the perception of the distinction between the Guṇas and the Spirit is liberation (mokṣa). Therefore, it has been said: 'This subtle body proceeds for the sake of the purpose of the Spirit.'"

Regarding the connection between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*): the cause refers to *dharma* and so forth, while the effect refers to ascending upwards and so forth, as we shall explain immediately hereafter. By way of this incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*), that is, by way of its application, [we consider] the connection with the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of *prakṛti*, the primary nature (*pradhāna*). Just as a king, due to his omnipresence within his own kingdom, does whatever he desires, so too, because of the connection with the omnipresence of *prakṛti* everywhere, there exists the relationship between cause and effect.
By way of elaboration, it establishes the distinct maintenance of separate bodies; it determines the state of the *liṅga*.

The *liṅga*—the subtle body accumulated from the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), endowed with the thirteenfold instruments—maintains its position within the wombs of humans, gods, and animals. How? Like an actor: just as an actor, having entered behind a curtain, emerges after becoming a god.
Again [it becomes] human, again Vidūṣaka;
thus, by way of the connection between the mark (*liṅga*), the cause (*nimitta*), and the effect (*naimittika*), having entered within the womb, it becomes an elephant, a woman, or a man.
It has been stated that the *liṅga*, permeated by dispositions (*bhāva*), transmigrates; as to what those dispositions are, he says:
The dispositions are innate, natural, and acquired—virtue and the rest;
they are observed as residing in the instruments (the senses) and as residing in the effects (the body), such as the embryo and so forth.
States of being are considered to be of three kinds: innate (*sāṃsiddhika*), natural (*prākṛta*), and modified (*vaikṛta*).

Among these, the innate are as follows: when Kapila, who had attained the state of a *bhava*, was born at the beginning of creation, four states arose simultaneously—dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty. The natural ones are described thus: the four sons of Brahmā, Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, and Sanatkumāra, came into being.
For those embodied beings who have arisen through the process of cause and effect and are sixteen years of age, these four states arise; therefore, they are called *prākṛta* (natural).

Likewise, there are the *vaikṛta* (modified) states, such as when our knowledge arises by taking the form of the Teacher as its instrumental cause (*nimitta*); from knowledge comes detachment (*vairāgya*), from detachment comes merit (*dharma*), and from merit comes sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
Since even the form of the Teacher is a modification (*vikṛti*), these states are called *vaikṛta*, by which the subtle body (*liṅga*) is perfumed (*adhivāsita*).

These four states transmigrate—those consisting of *sattva*, those consisting of *tamas*, and their opposites. It has already been explained here that "this form is *sāttvika*; from this, the *tāmasa* is the reverse. Thus, there are eight states: virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), power (*aiśvarya*), non-virtue (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), passion (*avairāgya*), and lack of power (*anaiśvarya*). This has been stated: "The intellect (*buddhi*) is determination; virtue, knowledge, and so forth are its functions. The body is the locus of these [functions]; the embryonic stages such as the *kalala* and so on, which were mentioned as being born of the mother, are the causes of growth in the union of semen and blood.

The stages beginning with the bubble (*budbuda*) and the lump of flesh (*māṃsapeśī*), as well as states such as childhood, youth, and old age, are produced on account of the essence of food and drink; therefore, they are said to depend upon the effect (*kāryāśrayiṇaḥ*). They arise caused by the enjoyment of objects such as food.
Regarding what was stated previously—that "by means of the connection between the cause and the effect"—it is here explained as follows: [the following verse].
By means of dharma there is upward movement; by means of adharma there is downward movement.
Through knowledge comes liberation, while from its opposite, bondage is held to arise.
"Going upwards by means of *dharma*": taking *dharma* as the cause, one leads [the self] upwards; "upwards" here refers to the eight stations (*sthāna*). They are as follows:

the station of Brahmā, of Prajāpati, of Soma, of Indra, of Gandharva, of Rakṣas, and of Piśāca. That subtle body goes there. In the case of animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and stationary beings, *adharma* is the cause.

Furthermore, through knowledge comes liberation (*apavarga*); that is, by means of the knowledge of the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*), liberation or *mokṣa* occurs, whereby the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) ceases and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is declared. Bondage is held to arise from the opposite [of knowledge]; ignorance is its cause, and this bondage—which is the effect of that cause—is said to be threefold: natural (*prākṛta*), modified (*vaikārika*), and personal (*dākṣiṇika*). This will be explained further on when it is stated: "By the natural bondage, as well as by the modified... and so forth.
"Bound by the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) through the third [state], one is not released by any other.
Furthermore, there is another sign:
"Dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) results from dispassion (*vairāgya*); cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) arises from passionate attachment (*rāga*)."
From sovereignty comes non-obstruction; from its opposite, the reverse occurs.

Just as someone may possess dispassion (*vairāgya*) but lacks knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), so from that dispassion preceded by ignorance, there occurs absorption into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*).

Upon death, he is absorbed into the eightfold nature—namely, into *pradhāna*, intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātras*)—but not into liberation; consequently, he transmigrates once again.

Likewise, this passionate attachment (*rājaso rāgaḥ*)—"I shall sacrifice, I shall give sacrificial fees, so that I may experience divine and human pleasures in this world or the next"—from such passionate attachment, transmigratory existence arises.

Likewise, from sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) comes non-obstruction (*avighāta*). This sovereignty consists of the eightfold qualities such as *aṇimā* and so forth; due to that cause of sovereignty, there is a resulting non-obstruction, meaning that one's sovereignty is not thwarted in the realms of Brahmā and others.

Furthermore, from the opposite [of sovereignty] comes the opposite: the non-obstruction of that [sovereignty] becomes its opposite, namely obstruction; due to a lack of sovereignty, one is obstructed everywhere.

Furthermore, there is another point: from perversion comes perversion; from the perversion of non-obstruction comes obstruction. Due to a lack of sovereignty, one is obstructed everywhere. (45) This sixteenfold set of effects, together with their causes, has been explained.
He asks: what is its nature? He says:
This is the creation of the intellect (pratyaya-sarga), known as error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment;
through the mutual suppression of the inequality of the qualities (guṇas), its subdivisions are fifty.
Just as this sixteenfold division of causes (*nimitta*) and effects (*naimittika*) has been explained, it is called the "evolution of the intellect" (*pratyayasarga*).

Since it has been stated that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the faculty of cognition (*pratyaya*), and that the intellect consists of determination (*adhyavasāya*), virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and so forth, this evolution of the intellect is divided into four types according to the distinctions known as error (*viparyaya*), incapacity (*aśakti*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and perfection (*siddhi*).
Among these, doubt is ignorance (*ajñāna*).
For example, when someone sees a post, there arises the doubt: "Is this a post or a person?
As for incapacity:
even after having correctly perceived that very post, one is unable to cut through the doubt; this is incapacity.
Thus, the third is called contentment (*tuṣṭi*); for example, one does not even wish to know or doubt that very post, thinking, "What is this to us?"—this is contentment.
The fourth is called attainment (*siddhi*); for example: [as follows].
One whose senses are delighted sees a creeper climbing a tree trunk or a bird; for him, there is the realization: "This is a tree trunk.
Thus, through the unequal distribution and mutual suppression of the qualities (*guṇa-vaiṣamya-vimarda*), there are fifty divisions of this fourfold creation of consciousness (*pratyaya-sarga*).
By that unequal distribution and suppression of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, there are these fifty varieties of that creation of consciousness.
In some cases, *sattva* is predominant while *rajas* and *tamas* remain indifferent; in some cases, *rajas*; and in some cases, *tamas*.
Thus, the divisions are stated:
there are five varieties of error (*viparyaya*), and [twenty-eight] varieties of incapacity (*aśakti*) arising from the impairment of the organs.
Contentment has twenty-eight varieties, while accomplishment is ninefold and eightfold.

There are five varieties of error: darkness (*tamas*), delusion (*moha*), great delusion (*mahāmoha*), gloom (*tāmisra*), and utter gloom (*andhatāmisra*). The diversity of these subdivisions will be explained immediately hereafter. Furthermore, there are twenty-eight varieties of incapacity due to the impairment of the instruments (*karaṇa*); we shall explain those as well. Likewise, contentment is ninefold; the *rājasa* forms of knowledge pertain to the upward-streaming (*ūrdhvasrotas*) path.
Similarly, the eightfold perfection (*siddhi*) consists of the *sāttvika* forms of knowledge, which likewise belong to that same upward-streaming path.

These will be explained in due order. [Verse 47] Now, the varieties of error (viparyaya) are stated: the division of darkness (tamas) is eightfold, that of delusion (moha) is likewise, and great delusion (mahāmoha) is tenfold.
Tāmisra is eighteenfold, and likewise, Andhatāmisra is so.

First, the division of *tamas* is eightfold; dissolution (*pralaya*) is distinguished from ignorance (*ajñāna*), and one dissolves into the eight primordial natures (*prakṛtis*)—namely, the *pradhāna*, intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*).
Therein, regarding the self as dissolved, one thinks, "I am liberated. This is the eightfold division of *tamas*; the meaning is that the division of *moha* is likewise eightfold.

Where there is the eightfold sovereignty consisting of *aṇimā* and so forth, the gods such as Indra do not attain liberation due to attachment to it, and upon its exhaustion, they transmigrate again; this is the eightfold delusion (*moha*).

The tenfold great delusion (*mahāmoha*) consists of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—these five objects of the gods characterized by pleasure—and for humans as well, these same five objects, sound and the rest, are likewise [sources of pleasure]; thus, among these ten, there is the great delusion.

Tāmisra is eighteenfold: the eightfold sovereignty and the ten objects of perception, both seen and heard. To rejoice in the prosperity of these eighteen and not to rejoice in their adversity—this is the eighteenfold *vikalpa* known as *tāmisra*. Likewise, *tāmisra* consists of the eightfold sovereignty and the ten objects of perception, both seen and heard; similarly, *andhatāmisra* also has eighteen divisions.

However, when there is the attainment of objects and during the time of enjoyment, he who dies or falls from the eightfold sovereign power (*aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya*) experiences great suffering; that is *andhatāmisra*.
Thus, the five types of error, beginning with *tamas*, when each is subdivided according to its variations, result in sixty-two varieties. // 48 //
The varieties of incapacity are now described:
incapacity is defined as the eleven impairments of the sense organs together with the impairments of the intellect;
these seventeen impairments of the intellect arise from the inversion of contentment and attainment.

It has been stated that there are twenty-eight varieties of incapacity (*aśakti*) arising from the impairment of the instruments [of perception]. Among these, the eleven impairments of the sense organs (*indriyavadha*) are: deafness, blindness, numbness, loss of taste, loss of smell, muteness, lameness, crookedness, lameness (in the sense of being unable to walk), impotence, and insanity.
Incapacity is said to be together with the impairments of the intellect (*buddhivadha*); thus, including those impairments of the intellect, there are twenty-eight varieties of incapacity.

The seventeen-fold division of the intellect (*buddhi*) consists of the divisions of contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and the divisions of attainment (*siddhi*), along with their opposites. There are nine divisions of contentment and eight divisions of attainment; these, together with their opposites, constitute eleven types. Thus, there are twenty-eight varieties known as incapacity (*aśakti*). From this error, the sequence of the divisions of attainment and contentment alone is to be understood. (49)
In that regard, contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is said to be ninefold:
four internal ones, known as those consisting of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), means (*upādāna*), time (*kāla*), and fortune (*bhāgya*);
and five external ones, arising from the cessation of objects (*viṣayoparama*). Thus, nine contentments are declared.

The four internal contentments (*ādhyātmika-tuṣṭi*) are those that arise within the self; they are called "internal. They are known as [contentment with] primordial nature (*prakṛti*), means (*upādāna*), time (*kāla*), and fortune (*bhāgya*). Among these, that which is called "primordial nature" is as follows: suppose someone understands primordial nature, as well as its qualified and unqualified states; having understood the reality and its effects, he is satisfied merely by that, yet for him there is no liberation.
This is the one called "primordial nature."

Regarding that which is called "appropriation" (*upādāna*): for example, someone who, without even understanding the principles (*tattva*), practices the grasping of appropriation—thinking that liberation comes from the triple staff, the water-pot, and the sectarian mark—for such a person there is no liberation, despite having this so-called "appropriation. Likewise, regarding that which is called "time" (*kāla*): the contentment consisting in the thought, "Liberation will come through time; what is the use of practicing the principles?"—for him there is no liberation despite having this so-called "time. Similarly, regarding that which is called "fortune" (*bhāgya*): the contentment consisting in the thought, "Liberation will come through fortune alone"—this is called "fortune."
Contentment is fourfold;
and there are five external [forms] due to the cessation from external objects.

The five external contentments arise from the cessation regarding sense-objects—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—due to seeing [the evils of] acquisition, preservation, loss, attachment, and injury.

For the sake of increase, cattle-rearing, trade, acceptance of gifts, and service must be performed; this acquisition is suffering. Once acquired, there is the suffering of preservation; because they are exhausted through enjoyment, there is the suffering of decay.
Likewise, when attachment to the enjoyment of sense-objects occurs, there is no tranquility of the senses—this is the fault of attachment.
Similarly, there is no enjoyment without harming living beings—this is the fault of violence.
Thus, from the perception of defects such as acquisition (*arjana*) and so forth, and from the cessation of the five objects of the senses, there are five contentments (*tuṣṭi*).
Accordingly, through the division into internal and external, there are nine contentments; their names are stated in another treatise as follows:
Ambhas, Salila, Ogha, Vṛṣṭi, Sutamas, Pāra, Sunetra, Nārīka, and Anuttamāmbhasika.
The obstructions to the intellect (*buddhibādha*) arise from the various forms of incapacity (*aśakti*) which are the opposites of these contentments (*tuṣṭi*).
For example, the obstructions to the intellect arise from such misconceptions as "there is no water," "there is no stream," and so forth.
Now, accomplishment (*siddhi*) is described.

Reasoning, oral instruction, study, the three types of removal of suffering, the acquisition of friends, and generosity—these are the eight accomplishments; the former three are the threefold goad for accomplishment.

Inference (*ūha*) is as follows: someone reflects, "What here is real? What is supreme? What is the highest good? How might I have accomplished my purpose? As he contemplates thus, knowledge arises: that the *puruṣa* is indeed distinct from primordial matter (*pradhāna*). There arises the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)—that the intellect (*buddhi*) is one thing, the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) another, and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs (*indriya*), and the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*) yet others—by which liberation is attained.
This first attainment is called "Inference" (ūha).

Likewise, from the knowledge of the Word (śabda), there arises knowledge whose objects are Nature (pradhāna), Spirit (puruṣa), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), the subtle elements (tanmātra), the senses, and the five gross elements; from that comes liberation—this is the attainment called "Word" (śabda).
From study—that is, from the study of the Vedas and other scriptures—one attains knowledge of the twenty-five principles and goes to liberation; this is the third attainment.

The threefold destruction of suffering consists in approaching a teacher for the sake of destroying the three types of suffering—internal, external, and celestial—and attaining liberation through his instruction; this is the fourth perfection (*siddhi*).
This very perfection is to be conceived as threefold according to the distinctions among the three types of suffering, thus making six perfections.
Likewise, the acquisition of a friend is when someone, having acquired knowledge from a friend, proceeds toward liberation; this is the seventh perfection.

Regarding generosity (*dāna*): just as someone, having assisted the Blessed Ones by giving them requisites such as a seat, medicinal herbs, a triple-staff, and a water-pot, as well as food and clothing, and thereby attaining knowledge from them, proceeds toward liberation—this is the eighth accomplishment (*siddhi*).

Regarding these eight accomplishments, other treatises have established the following designations: *Tāra*, *Sutāra*, *Tāratāra*, *Pramoda*, *Pramudita*, *Pramodamāna*, *Ramyaka*, and *Sadāpramudita*.

The opposites of these [contentments] are the bondages of the intellect (*buddhi-bandha*). Those which are the reverse [of the contentments] are assigned to incapacity (*aśakti*); they should be understood as "not crossing over," "crossing with difficulty," "not crossing at all," and so forth.
These twenty-eight varieties of incapacity have been stated; when combined with the bondages of the intellect, they constitute the eleven bondages of the organs (*indriya-bandha*).
Among these, there are nine opposites of contentment and eight opposites of the perfections (*siddhi*); thus, these seventeen are the bondages of the intellect.

Together with these, the twenty-eight varieties of incapacity (*aśakti*), which consist of the bondage of the organs, have been explained later; thus, the enumeration and detailed exposition have been made specifically for error (*viparyaya*), incapacity (*aśakti*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and attainment (*siddhi*). Furthermore, that which precedes attainment is the threefold "goad" (*aṅkuśa*); those [factors] which precede attainment are error, incapacity, and contentment.

Thus, the goad for success (*siddhi*) is of three kinds according to its divisions; just as an elephant becomes submissive when seized by a goad, so too the world, when seized by error (*viparyaya*), incapacity (*aśakti*), and contentment (*tuṣṭi*), falls into ignorance. Therefore, having abandoned these, success should be cultivated;
from that success, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) arises, and that is liberation (*mokṣa*). // 51 //

Now, regarding what was stated—that the *liṅga* is permeated by dispositions (*bhāva*)—therein the dispositions were said to be the eight factors beginning with *dharma*, which are modifications of the intellect (*buddhi*) resulting from the transformations of error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment; this is called the "dispositional creation" (*pratyayasarga*). Furthermore, the "subtle-element creation" (*tanmātrasarga*), consisting of the fourteen elements ending with the gross elements, has also been described. To the question, "Since the purpose of the *puruṣa* is accomplished by one kind of creation alone, what is the use of both types of creation?", he says:
There is no gender-sign without entities, nor is there the manifestation of entities without a gender-sign;
therefore, creation proceeds in two ways: that called "gender" and that called "entity."

Without the dispositions (*bhāva*), which are the creation of the intellect (*pratyayasarga*), there is no subtle body (*liṅga*); nor is there the creation of the subtle elements (*tanmātrasarga*), because the acquisition of each subsequent body is caused by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) and unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of each preceding one.

Without the subtle body and the creation of the subtle elements, there is no manifestation of the dispositions, because virtue (*dharma*) and the rest are accomplished through the gross and subtle bodies, and because the cycle of creation is beginningless.
Thus, the mutual dependence of the seed and the sprout is not a logical fault, since it pertains to the respective species, even though specific individuals depend upon one another.
Because they are mutually independent, therefore the creation proceeds as twofold: that which is called "existence" (bhāva) and that which is called "the marks" (liṅga).
Furthermore:
the divine [creation] consists of eight varieties, and the animal [creation] is fivefold.
And the human realm is of one kind; briefly stated, this is the elemental creation.
Among those, the divine (daiva) is of eight kinds: Brāhma, Prājāpatya, Saumya, Aindra, Gāndharva, Yākṣa, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca.
The animal kingdom (tairaśca) is fivefold, consisting of the beings that are cattle, wild animals, birds, reptiles, and immobile things.
The human womb is only one. Thus, there are fourteen types of beings.
The three qualities (guṇas) exist in all three worlds; among them, it is said that which is predominant where?
The creation at the top is predominantly characterized by *sattva*, and that at the root is predominantly characterized by *tamas*;
in the middle, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, it is predominantly characterized by *rajas*.
"Upward" refers to the eight abodes of the gods; there, *sattva* is vast, extensive, predominant, and thus it is called "upward *sattva*.
Even there, however, *rajas* and *tamas* exist.
At the root, from animals down to immobile beings, the entire creation is pervaded by a predominance of *tamas*; even there, however, *sattva* and *rajas* exist.
In the midst of the human state, passion (*rajas*) is predominant; even there, goodness (*sattva*) and darkness (*tamas*) are present. Therefore, human beings consist mostly of suffering.
Thus, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—meaning from the creator Brahmā down to the stationary objects—is the nature of existence.

In this way, the non-material creation, the creation of the subtle body (*liṅga-sarga*), the creation of dispositions (*bhāva-sarga*), and the creation of the elements (*bhūta-sarga*)—namely, the divine, human, and animal births—this is the sixteenfold creation produced by *pradhāna*. (54)
In that state, the conscious person experiences suffering caused by old age and death;
therefore, in brief, suffering exists as long as the subtle body has not ceased.

In this context, among those [categories]—the divine, human, and animal births—it is the conscious *puruṣa*, the possessor of sentience, who experiences the suffering caused by old age and death; it is not the *pradhāna*, nor the intellect (*buddhi*), nor the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), nor the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), nor the senses, nor the gross elements.
He now distinguishes for how long the *puruṣa* experiences this suffering.

Because the *liṅga* has not ceased, that which consists of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth—which, having entered the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), becomes manifest therein—remains until it ceases;

this is what is called the "cycle-of-existence body. In brief, in these three locations, the person experiences the suffering caused by old age and death as long as the *liṅga* has not ceased—that is, until the cessation of the *liṅga*.
Upon the cessation of the *liṅga* (the subtle body), there is liberation; upon the attainment of liberation, there is no suffering.

By what, then, is that [subtle body] ceased? When there is knowledge of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), characterized by the discernment of the difference between *sattva* (pure consciousness) and the *puruṣa* (the Self)—namely:
"this is *pradhāna* (primordial matter), this is *buddhi* (intellect), this is *ahaṃkāra* (ego), these are the five *tanmātras* (subtle elements), the eleven organs, and the five gross elements."
From the knowledge that "the Puruṣa is other than these and dissimilar [to them]," there is the cessation of the marks [of worldly existence], and from that, liberation.
It is now stated what the cause of the process of manifestation (pravṛtti) is, beginning from what:
this [process] is produced by Prakṛti, extending from Mahat down to the objects consisting of the gross elements.
For the sake of the liberation of each individual, the undertaking for the sake of others is like that for one's own sake.

Thus, this—referring both to completion and to instruction—is the undertaking regarding the primary cause and its transformations, the primary cause and its operations, which extends from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the specific gross elements: from the Primary Cause comes the Great Principle; from the Great Principle, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra); from that, the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the eleven organs;
and from the subtle elements, the five gross elements. This process exists for the sake of the liberation of each individual soul, leading the soul through the states of gods, humans, and animals.

How can an undertaking for the sake of liberation by those who have already attained it be considered as if it were for one's own benefit? Just as someone might abandon their own interest to perform a service for a friend, so it is with *pradhāna*.
In this case, the *puruṣa* renders no reciprocal benefit whatsoever to the *pradhāna*.

Self-interest is not truly self-interest; rather, the true interest is solely the interest of another. This consists in the perception of objects such as sound and the like, as well as the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*.
In the three worlds, the *puruṣas* are to be joined with objects such as sound, and finally with liberation (*mokṣa*). Such is the activity of *pradhāna*, and it has been said:
"Like a potter, *pradhāna* ceases its activity once the purpose of the *puruṣa* has been accomplished. (56)

To this it is replied: "The *pradhāna* is insentient and the *puruṣa* is sentient; [it acts] with the thought, 'I must join the *puruṣa* with objects such as sound in the three worlds, and in the end, liberation must be brought about'—how can there be such activity as if it were sentient? True, but activity and cessation are observed even among insentient things; therefore, he says: [He gives examples: Just as milk flows for the sake of the calf, as food and drink act for the sake of a living being, as grass and earth act for the sake of a cow, so too does the insentient *pradhāna* act for the sake of the *puruṣa*. Just as a magnet attracts iron without consciousness, so too does the *pradhāna* act toward the *puruṣa*. Thus, although the *pradhāna* is insentient, its activity and cessation are established through its conjunction with the *puruṣa*. Therefore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the capacity for activity, just like a chariot and its driver. For example, a chariot by itself cannot proceed on a road without a driver, nor can a driver proceed without a chariot; when both are joined, they proceed together. Similarly, the *pradhāna* is like the chariot and the *puruṣa* is like the driver; thus, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. Moreover, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the quality of being an object, just like a woman and her husband. For example, a woman who is an object of desire acts for the sake of her husband, and a husband likewise acts for the sake of his wife; in the same way, the *pradhāna* is the object of the *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣa* is the subject. Therefore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the quality of being a means, just like a servant and his master. For example, a servant acts for the sake of his master, and a master likewise acts for the sake of his servant; in the same way, the *pradhāna* is the means for the *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣa* is the end. Therefore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. And finally, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the quality of being a cause, just like a seed and its sprout. For example, a seed acts for the sake of the sprout, and a sprout likewise acts for the sake of the seed; in the same way, the *pradhāna* is the cause of the *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣa* is the effect. Therefore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the quality of being a support, just like a wall and a painting. For example, a wall acts for the sake of a painting, and a painting likewise acts for the sake of the wall; in the same way, the *pradhāna* is the support for the *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣa* is the supported. Therefore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the quality of being a locus, just like a mirror and a reflection. For example, a mirror acts for the sake of a reflection, and a reflection likewise acts for the sake of the mirror; in the same way, the *pradhāna* is the locus for the *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣa* is the located. Therefore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the quality of being a field, just like a field and a farmer. For example, a field acts for the sake of a farmer, and a farmer likewise acts for the sake of the field; in the same way, the *pradhāna* is the field for the *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣa* is the farmer. Therefore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the quality of being a vessel, just like a vessel and its contents. For example, a vessel acts for the sake of its contents, and contents likewise act for the sake of the vessel; in the same way, the *pradhāna* is the vessel for the *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣa* is the contents. Therefore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the quality of being a source, just like a mine and its ore. For example, a mine acts for the sake of its ore, and ore likewise acts for the sake of the mine; in the same way, the *pradhāna* is the source of the *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣa* is the extracted product. Therefore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the quality of being a manifestation, just like a dream and a dreamer. For example, a dream acts for the sake of a dreamer, and a dreamer likewise acts for the sake of the dream; in the same way, the *pradhāna* is the manifestation for the *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣa* is the witness. Therefore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the quality of being a transformation, just like clay and a potter. For example, clay acts for the sake of a potter, and a potter likewise acts for the sake of the clay; in the same way, the *pradhāna* is the material cause for the *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣa* is the agent of transformation. Therefore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the quality of being a substrate, just like a body and a soul. For example, a body acts for the sake of a soul, and a soul likewise acts for the sake of the body; in the same way, the *pradhāna* is the substrate for the *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣa* is the substratum. Therefore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the quality of being a power, just like a weapon and a warrior. For example, a weapon acts for the sake of a warrior, and a warrior likewise acts for the sake of the weapon; in the same way, the *pradhāna* is the power of the *puruṣa*, and the *puruṣa* is the possessor of power. Therefore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because it possesses the quality of being a purpose, just like a sacrifice and a sacrificer. For example, a sacrifice
Just as the flow of milk from the insentient [cow] occurs for the sake of the growth of the calf,
so does the activity of the Pradhāna occur for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa.

Just as grass and other fodder, having been eaten by a cow, transform into the state of milk and cause the growth of the calf, and once the calf is nourished, [the milk] ceases; in the same way, the primary cause (*pradhāna*) acts for the sake of the liberation of the person (*puruṣa*), and thus the activity of the ignorant one [ceases when that purpose is achieved]. // 57 // Furthermore:
Just as people engage in activities for the sake of satisfying their longing,
so too does the Unmanifest act for the sake of the liberation of the Person.

Just as in the world, when there is a desire for something, one engages in activities to achieve its cessation, and having completed the task, one desists from the activities of going and coming; so too, for the sake of the liberation of the *puruṣa*, the *pradhāna*—having accomplished both types of the *puruṣa*'s purpose, namely the perception of the enjoyment of objects such as sound and the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*—desists. // 58 //
Moreover:
Just as a dancer ceases from her dance after displaying herself to the audience,
so does Nature cease after manifesting herself to the Spirit.

Just as an actress, having displayed on the stage performances consisting of songs and instrumental music composed of the sentiments (*rasa*) such as the erotic and the mental states (*bhāva*) such as history, ceases from dancing once her task is accomplished; so too does *prakṛti*, having manifested herself to the *puruṣa* through the distinctions of intellect, ego, the subtle elements, the senses, and the gross elements, desists. 59.
How, or what, could there be a cause for turning back? To this he says:
Through various means, she who is beneficial acts for the sake of that man who is ungrateful and devoid of virtue; though she herself possesses virtues, her actions for him are rendered fruitless.

By various means, Nature (prakṛti) acts as a benefactor to the Spirit (puruṣa), who is himself non-beneficial; how so? By manifesting herself through the states of gods, humans, and animals; by the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion; and by the nature of objects such as sound and the rest—thus, by these various means, having revealed herself, she ceases [her activity] with the thought, "I am one, you are another. Therefore, for the sake of that eternal Spirit, she performs both purposeful and purposeless actions, and she acts just like some person.

One who assists others benefits everyone but does not seek any return for himself; such is his nature. [The *puruṣa*] effects the purpose of the *puruṣa*, yet performs what is ultimately useless. Having previously stated that it ceases after manifesting itself, [the author] now asks: once it has ceased, what does it do? He says: 60. One who assists others benefits everyone but does not seek any return for himself; such is his nature. [The *puruṣa*] effects the purpose of the *puruṣa*, yet performs what is ultimately useless. Having previously stated that it ceases after manifesting itself, [the author] now asks: once it has ceased, what does it do? He says:
"It is my conviction that there is nothing more subtle than Prakṛti;
once she has been seen [by the Puruṣa], thinking 'I have been seen,' she does not present herself to the Puruṣa's sight again."

"It is my conviction that there is nothing in the world more delicate than primordial nature (prakṛti); for this reason, the thought has arisen in her solely for the sake of another: 'Why have I been seen by this Puruṣa? Thus she no longer comes into the sight of this Puruṣa;
the meaning is that she attains non-perception by the Puruṣa."
In that regard, he describes a more subtle [view]:
they declare Īśvara to be the cause, saying:
"This living being is unborn and not its own master; this self of ours goes to heaven or indeed to hell, impelled by Īśvara."
Others, proponents of intrinsic nature as the cause, say:
"By what have the swans been made white? By what have the peacocks been made variegated?
It is by intrinsic nature alone."

On this point, the Sāṃkhya teachers say: since the Lord is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), how could beings endowed with qualities (*saguṇa*) be born from him? Or rather, why would it not be more logical for them to arise from *prakṛti*, which is likewise devoid of qualities? Just as from white threads only a white cloth arises, and from black [threads] only a black one.

Thus, it is understood that from the Pradhāna, which consists of the three guṇas, the three worlds—which likewise consist of the three guṇas—have arisen. Since Īśvara is devoid of guṇas, it is illogical for the worlds, which possess guṇas, to originate from him. By this, the Puruṣa is also explained.
Likewise, it has been stated that for some, time is the cause:
"Time exists as the five elements; time destroys the world;
time remains awake while others sleep; indeed, time is difficult to overcome."

"The manifest, the unmanifest, and the Puruṣa—these are the three categories. Therefore, time is included therein; it is manifest because it is the agent of all things. Furthermore, Primordial Matter (pradhāna) alone is the cause even of time, and inherent nature (svabhāva) is likewise absorbed right here. Consequently, time is not the cause, nor is inherent nature."
Therefore, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) alone is the cause; there is no other cause for primordial nature.
Furthermore, the vision [of nature] does not recur for the *puruṣa*.
Hence, it is my conviction that there exists no cause whatsoever—such as a Lord (*īśvara*) or the like—that is more delicate or more enjoyable than primordial nature. (61)
And thus it is established in the verse:
"The person is liberated, the person is one who transmigrates"—so it is declared.
Therefore, no one at all is bound, nor is anyone liberated, nor does anyone transmigrate.
Prakṛti, having various supports, transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated.

For that reason, the Puruṣa is neither bound nor liberated, nor does it transmigrate; rather, it is Prakṛti alone— which assumes various bases such as the divine, human, and animal wombs— that is bound, liberated, and transmigrates by way of the nature of the intellect, ego, subtle elements, senses, and gross elements.

Now, if he is already liberated by nature and all-pervading, how can he transmigrate— since transmigration is for the purpose of attaining what has not yet been attained? It is because of that [buddhi] by which it is designated that "the person is bound," "the person is liberated," or "he transmigrates"— even though the state of being a transmigrator does not actually exist in the person—
that the true nature of the person is manifested through the knowledge of the distinction between the *sattva* (buddhi) and the person (*puruṣa*).
When that [nature] is manifested, the Puruṣa is alone, pure, liberated, and established in its own nature.
Here, if there is no bondage for the Puruṣa, then there is also no liberation.

To this it is replied: Nature itself binds and liberates itself; wherein the subtle body—consisting of the subtle elements and endowed with the threefold instruments—is bound by the threefold bondage.

And it has been said: "Bound by the natural (prākṛta) bond, as well as by the modified (vaikārika), and by the third, the sacrificial (dākṣiṇa) bond—one is not released by any other means. That subtle body is conjoined with merit and demerit. (62)
It is asked: "How is it that primordial nature (prakṛti) is bound, primordial nature is liberated, and primordial nature transmigrates? It is replied:
"In this way, primordial nature binds itself by itself through seven forms;
and for the sake of the Puruṣa's purpose, that very same [nature] liberates itself by means of a single form."

These seven are said to consist of exactly seven forms: virtue (dharma), dispassion (vairāgya), power (aiśvarya), vice (adharma), ignorance (ajñāna), passion (avairāgya), and lack of power (anaiśvarya). These are the seven forms of Prakṛti; by means of them, Prakṛti binds her very self.
That same Prakṛti, thinking "the purpose of the Puruṣa (puruṣārtha) must be accomplished," liberates her own self through the single form of knowledge.
How does that knowledge arise?
Thus, through the practice of reality, there arises a complete knowledge—free from error and pure—that "I am not," "nothing is mine," and "I do not exist. // ISk_64 //

Through the practice of contemplating the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) in the manner thus described, there arises in the person (*puruṣa*) this knowledge: "This is *prakṛti*, this is the *puruṣa*, and these are the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs, and the gross elements. [He realizes: "I do not exist as a non-existent; this body is not mine, because I am one thing and the body is another; I am not the body. This knowledge is complete, free from egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), and entirely pure due to being free from error.

Through the absence of error and the absence of doubt, that very knowledge which is pure and absolute arises and becomes manifest—the knowledge of the twenty-five principles belonging to the Puruṣa; there is nothing else that is the cause of liberation. (64) What does the Puruṣa do with respect to this knowledge?
Thereby, the Puruṣa, established in his own state like a spectator, beholds Nature (prakṛti), which has ceased its productivity by the force of its purpose and has withdrawn from the seven forms.

By means of that pure, absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*), the Person (*puruṣa*) perceives *prakṛti*, remaining like a spectator—standing as one who is self-abiding (*svastha*). Just as a spectator standing in the theater watches a dancer, so too the self-abiding one remains within himself;
"self-abiding" means established in his own place.

Of what nature is this Prakṛti? It is "nivṛttaprasavā," meaning its procreative activity has ceased because it has turned away from the purposeless effects of the intellect (buddhi) and ego (ahaṃkāra). It is "saptarūpavinivṛttā," meaning it has desisted from the seven forms. One perceives Prakṛti as having withdrawn from those seven forms—virtue (dharma) and the rest—by which she binds herself, once the dual purposes of the Puruṣa have been accomplished. // 65 //
Furthermore:
"One [Puruṣa] becomes indifferent, thinking 'I have seen her'; the other ceases [to act], thinking 'I have been seen.
Even though their union exists, there is no further purpose for creation. (ISk 66)
"Just as one who stands on the stage"—meaning, just like a spectator standing on the stage—so too the Puruṣa is solitary, alone, and pure.
Thinking, "I have been seen by him," Nature (Prakṛti) desists and ceases; she is one and only one, the primary cause even of the three worlds.

There is no second Nature, for there is no difference in kind despite the difference in form. Thus, even when the union of Nature and Puruṣa has ceased, [the Puruṣa remains] because of its all-pervasiveness.

There is conjunction, but creation does not arise from conjunction alone. Even though a conjunction exists between those two—prakṛti and puruṣa—it is because both are all-pervading that there is no further purpose for creation once it has already occurred, since the aim of prakṛti has been fulfilled. Prakṛti’s purpose is twofold: the perception of objects of sound and the other sense-objects, and the perception of the distinction between the guṇas and the puruṣa.
Since the purpose of creation has been fulfilled in both cases, there is no further motive for a renewed creation.

Just as between a creditor and a debtor, once the object of the transaction has been purified through the act of giving and receiving, no further connection of interest remains despite their continued association;
likewise, there is no further purpose for the union of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. (66)
If liberation appears when knowledge has arisen for a person, one might ask: "Why does it not happen for me? To this it is said:

"Upon the attainment of perfect knowledge, when dharma and the other [factors] no longer function as causes, the body continues to be sustained by the force of the formative predispositions (*saṃskāra*), like the spinning of a wheel. (ISk 67)

Although the knowledge of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) constitutes perfect knowledge, nevertheless, by the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), the yogi remains with his body maintained. How so? Like the whirling of a wheel (*cakrabhrama*). Just as a potter, having set the wheel spinning, makes a jar—having placed a lump of clay upon the wheel and fashioned it into a jar, he then releases it—and yet the wheel continues to spin; so too does the yogi remain.

Precisely through the power of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), once right knowledge has been attained, for one who has produced that right knowledge, the factors such as merit (*dharma*) no longer function as causes;

these seven forms, which constitute bonds, have been burnt away by right knowledge. Just as seeds burnt by fire are no longer capable of sprouting, so too these bonds—merit and the rest—are no longer capable [of producing further existence].

When dharma and the other factors have ceased to function as causes, the soul remains with its body sustained by the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*). Why does the destruction of present dharma and adharma not occur through knowledge? Precisely because they are present; they reach destruction in the very next moment. Knowledge, however, burns away future karma, as well as that which one performs with the present body, because it effects the performance of prescribed duties. Thus, upon the fall of the body due to the exhaustion of residual impressions, liberation (*mokṣa*) occurs. // 67 //
What kind of state does he attain? It is said:
upon the dissolution of the body, having accomplished his purpose, and with the cessation of primordial matter (pradhāna), he attains both the certain and the absolute liberation (kaivalya).

Upon the dissolution of the body, attained through the exhaustion of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by merit and demerit, and because the *pradhāna* has fulfilled its purpose and ceased its activity, one attains absolute, certain, ultimate, and uninterrupted isolation (*kaivalya*). Because of this state of being solitary, liberation is achieved;
thus, one attains that distinguished isolation which is both absolute and ultimate. (68)
This secret knowledge of the goals of human life has been fully declared by the Supreme Seer;
herein, the stability, origin, and dissolution of all beings are contemplated.
Liberation is the goal of human endeavor; for that purpose, this secret and esoteric knowledge was fully expounded by the supreme seer, the venerable Kapila seer.
In this knowledge, the maintenance, origination, and dissolution—the persistence, manifestation, and disappearance—of all beings, which are modifications of nature, are contemplated and investigated.
Through the investigation of these, a thorough realization consisting of the discernment of the twenty-five principles is accomplished. // 69 //
The Sāṃkhya system was indeed proclaimed by the sage Kapila as the cause of liberation from saṃsāra;
herein are these seventy Āryā verses, and the commentary upon them composed by Gauḍapāda.
The Sage, out of compassion, bestowed this supreme purifier upon Āsuri; Āsuri, in turn, gave it to Pañcaśikha, and by him the Tantra was widely propagated.
This [Sāṃkhya system], which has come down through a succession of disciples, was correctly understood by Īśvarakṛṣṇa,
who possessed noble intelligence, and then condensed into these Āryā verses as a definitive conclusion.
It is said that the seventy topics contained therein are the topics of the entire *Ṣaṣṭitantra*,
excluding the illustrative narratives and devoid of the arguments of opponents.
